textHeavy: Lines 408-472, about 866 words, the longest stretch in the lesson. It runs from the end of the code example to the first InterviewQuestionPlayground. It covers: why the boundary value 100 found the bug (408-410); 'How to triage a late bug', 5 steps, and the checklist (412-425); and all four Push Further sections: 'Designing for fixability' (429-437: spare cells, defeature bits, patch paths, the trade-off), 'Reading the industry data' (439-448: the WRG 2022 numbers and their caveats), 'Sign-off is a judgement, not a number' (450-460: the evidence a review weighs) and 'Shift-left trade-offs' (462-467). There is no visual, table or code anywhere in it.

Lines 7-20, Quick Take, about 352 words. Defines a bug, tape-out and a respin, gives the WRG numbers (about 24% first-silicon success, about 1:1 verification to design engineers) and the crash-test analogy with where it breaks, then the four objectives and the prerequisites. Only <BeforeYouStart/> and the 'Words you will meet' table follow it.

Lines 181-199, about 345 words between <HallOfShameCarousel/> and the lifecycle SVG. 'What each card teaches' explains why FDIV, Ariane 501 and Spectre/Meltdown escaped and the missing check for each, plus the common thread (the plan never asked the question; 'passing simulation means correct silicon'). Then the five-step lifecycle list with owners (spec, vplan, testbench, regression, sign-off) and the two feedback loops.

Lines 46-64, about 339 words: 'The Multi-Million Dollar Question' plus the opening of 'The design–verification gap', before <DesignGapChart/>. It covers WRG headcount (1:1 mean peak, 5-to-1 for processors, 49% of designers' time), why fabricated logic cannot be patched, metal-only vs full respin vs firmware/defeature workarounds, the three respin costs (masks/NRE, time, market window), 24% first-silicon success with logic/functional flaws leading, and the NRE callout.

Lines 319-339, about 265 words (just under the threshold). The DV career ladder, 'Why verification effort rivals design effort' (four bullets), the four-bullet Recap and the Make It Work intro, between the roles table and the worked-example table.

Lines 164-178, about 212 words (below the threshold, but dense new concepts). FIB edit, firmware/microcode workaround, defeature ('chicken') bit, what makes a bug ECO-able, the two pitfalls (every fix needs a full respin; a FIB edit fixes the product) and the carousel intro.

needs.where: ### Fixing silicon: ECO, metal-only respin or full respin (lines 94-173); reused under 'Worked example: four late bugs, four decisions' (338-351) and 'How to triage a late bug' (412-418)
needs.concept: Which production fix a bug gets: pre-tape-out ECO, metal-only respin (rewiring plus spare cells, held wafers), full base-layer respin, or a firmware/defeature workaround now with the real fix later. The decision depends on whether masks exist yet, whether the fix needs new transistors, and whether it fits in the spare cells within reach and still closes timing. This is the misconception 'every silicon fix needs a full respin'.
needs.interaction: New FixPathDecisionLab (model src/lib/fix-path-model.ts, a pure decision function; tests in tests/lib/fix-path-model.test.ts). Presets are the four worked-example bugs: wrong reset value 3 weeks before tape-out; > vs >= with spare cells nearby; a new pipeline stage of several hundred flip-flops; field corruption with a defeature bit. A Custom mode exposes the facts as toggles: taped out yes/no, needs new transistors yes/no, gates needed vs spare cells nearby, timing closes yes/no/unknown, firmware or defeature path available. The learner first commits a prediction of the production fix. The reveal then shows: (1) the same three-band layer cross-section the lesson's SVG uses (hatched = new mask, solid = reused/held wafer, dashed = no mask yet); (2) the triage decision tree with the path taken highlighted, as steps 2 to 4 of 'How to triage'; (3) the rule-of-thumb multiplier and stage, read from src/lib/bug-cost-model.ts (no new numbers); (4) a qualitative delay class (days to weeks / weeks / months / 'workaround as fast as a firmware release; real fix waits for new silicon'); (5) an escape-analysis line naming the earlier activity that should have caught it. If timing is unknown the result must be 'depends': metal-only if physical design finds a timing-clean fix, otherwise a full respin. Kata 3 needs exactly that nuance. Option feedback diagnoses 'lines of RTL = layers', 'FIB fixes production' and 'any bug can be fixed in metal'. Fidelity: conceptual illustration of industry practice. No file in sources/ covers ECO or respin practice, so the model may encode only what the lesson already states. No dollar figures, no mask counts, no node-specific claims. Keyboard: SegmentedControl and buttons; readable at 390 px with the cross-section stacked above the tree.

needs.where: ### Shift left and the verification lifecycle: shift-left table and SVG (lines 249-304)
needs.concept: Shift left: each kind of bug has an earliest activity that catches it reliably (planning at spec review catches spec contradictions; lint catches latches and width mismatches; block simulation catches block functional bugs; block formal catches arbiter/FIFO/FSM corner cases; emulation catches boot and driver hangs). Cutting an activity does not remove its bugs. They move right, to stages that cost about ×10 more each. Covers the misconception 'verification is overhead we can cut'.
needs.interaction: New ShiftLeftTimeline (model src/lib/shift-left-model.ts). Bug kind -> activities that catch it -> the stage each activity runs at -> multiplier from bug-cost-model. The bug kinds and their mappings come only from the lesson's table and quiz question 10. The view is one project timeline (spec, RTL, integration, tape-out line, silicon, field) with six bug tokens. The learner switches activities on and off: planning, lint, block simulation, block formal, emulation. Before each run they predict where a chosen bug will now be found. The reveal moves each token to the earliest enabled catcher and shows that stage's ×N. With every activity off, the tokens pile up after the tape-out line. Preset 'schedule slipped, cut regressions' shows the overhead mistake. A second toggle shows that the late stages still run and catch what only they can (block interactions, real software), which is the lesson's pitfall that shift left does not remove the late stages. Stepped transitions only, with motion-reduce; text list of token positions for screen readers. The nearest existing visual is VerificationMethodologiesDiagram (F1B), but it has no planning or lint, no bug kinds and no multipliers, and F1B owns it.

needs.where: ## Practice & Reinforce > ### Estimation kata: four bugs, one ranking (lines 636-659)
needs.concept: The spine card's required hands-on: for 4 bug scenarios, choose ECO vs respin, then rank the five discovery stages by cost and by delay. The two rankings differ for a field bug with a workaround.
needs.interaction: A mode='kata' of FixPathDecisionLab on the four kata scenarios: FIFO write-when-full gap at spec review; interrupt cleared one cycle early, 3 weeks before tape-out; 40 gates needed with 12 spare cells nearby; DMA started within two cycles of wake, with no defeature bit but boot firmware that can wait. Answers stay hidden until the learner commits a fix for each. Then comes a keyboard-operable ordering task (move up/down buttons, no drag-only): rank spec review, RTL simulation, full-chip/emulation, post-silicon and field by cost, then by delay. The check shows the order from bug-cost-model and explains the delay exception: field containment can be fast while the real fix waits for silicon. The <details> worked solution stays as the text equivalent.

needs.where: ## Make It Work > ### Worked example: the same mistake at the cheapest stage (lines 353-410)
needs.concept: Boundary-value testing: the one-character > vs >= bug is invisible to typical values (50, 150) and caught only at the exact boundary (100). It is the cheapest-stage version of worked bug 2 and makes the interview's 'edge case' concrete.
needs.interaction: New BoundaryProbe (model src/lib/boundary-probe-model.ts, about 20 lines plus tests). An 8-bit number line from 0 to 255 shows the spec region (temp >= 100) and the RTL region (temp > 100, or >= after a 'Fix the RTL' toggle). The learner picks test values: preset 'typical' 50 and 150, preset 'boundary' 99, 100 and 101 (the lesson's test), or custom chips. They predict the PASS/FAIL counts, then see a ✓ or ✕ on each value with alarm vs expected, plus the summary line (PASS=2 FAIL=1, and PASS=3 FAIL=0 after the fix), which must match the lesson's hand-traced output. The disagreement band is exactly one value wide. Semantics: IEEE 1800-2023 11.4.4 (relational operators yield 1'b0/1'b1 for known operands and compare unsigned when either operand is unsigned) and 11.4.5 (!== compares including x and z). Do not add an X input here. With temp = X, both alarm and expected become 1'bx (11.4.4) and alarm !== expected is 0, so the check would PASS. That trap belongs to F2A's LogicStateDiagram, not to an orientation lesson.

needs.where: ## Push Further > ### Expert: Sign-off is a judgement, not a number (lines 450-460), inside the 866-word stretch
needs.concept: Tape-out sign-off weighs evidence: plan completeness, coverage with reviewed exclusions, regression stability across seeds, a falling bug-discovery rate, open bugs with workarounds and explicit risk decisions, formal assumptions and emulation results. The classic failure is 100% coverage of an incomplete plan.
needs.interaction: New SignoffReviewBoard (pure data model src/lib/signoff-scenarios.ts). Three or four preset projects are shown as evidence dashboards. Presets: the interview case, 92% coverage with 3 medium bugs, workaround known vs unknown; 100% coverage, but the plan has no scenario for a feature; a flat bug-discovery trend; seed-unstable regressions. The learner decides 'tape out', 'tape out with explicit waivers' or 'not yet, target these holes'. Feedback names the evidence they overlooked. Fidelity: conceptual illustration. The lesson states that no standard defines sign-off criteria, so presets must not claim thresholds and must say 'project-dependent'.

needs.where: ### A test must be able to fail, L119-136 (the four silent failures); Make It Work Step 3, L619-647 (the WRAP_AT(6) mutant and 'How to do it on any block'); Push Further 'Expert: Qualifying the testbench', L689-694
needs.concept: A self-checking test is evidence only if it can fail. The bench-side silent failures are a compare that is missing or disabled, a compare against a copy of the DUT's own output, and an X-blind !=. Mutation testing proves a check can fail: inject a bug, see FAIL, revert, see PASS. A mutant that survives points at a weak check or a plan hole.
needs.interaction: 'Can this bench fail?' lab on the Make It Work bench. The learner picks a DUT variant: correct WRAP_AT(7); mutant WRAP_AT(6); rst never asserted, so count stays X (counter-bug-model nextCount already models X per §12.4); or 'reset ignored mid-count'. The compare form is a control rendered inside the code line: `count !== expected`, `count != expected`, compare commented out, or `expected = count` (self-copy). Before Run, the learner predicts the two printed lines (PASS=n FAIL=m, COVERAGE seen_max=k). They then step through the 20 checks with PlaybackControls. A waveform shows count (ACT, solid) against expected (EXP, dashed), with a check marker at each falling edge (✓/✕). An X check shows that != gives 1'bx (§11.4.5), so the if takes the else branch and pass_cnt++ (§12.4). A BlockDiagram copy of the lesson's anatomy diagram marks the broken part in its error state. Matrix mode crosses every compare form with every mutant (caught or survived), and adds the plan rows with their coverage counts, so the 'Reset mid-count' row shows 0 hits and its mutant survives. Accuracy: the lab must reproduce the lesson exactly. That means PASS=20 FAIL=0 seen_max=2 for the correct DUT, and PASS=7 FAIL=13 seen_max=0 with the first failure at 80 ns for WRAP_AT(6). A stuck-X DUT with != prints PASS=20 FAIL=0: the bench's if/else counts a PASS, while debug-challenge item 4 has no else and so counts nothing. With !== it prints FAIL=20. Build it as a pure model, src/lib/counter-bench-model.ts, layered on counter-bug-model (simulateCounter already takes an rst schedule) and on sv-four-state-model compare/ifBranch/add. Map check i to the value after rising edge i.

needs.where: ### Directed, constrained-random and formal, L151-170, plus the hand-written methods SVG figure L171-375 (about 200 lines of literal rect/text) and its debrief L375
needs.concept: Directed testing finds what you imagine, random finds what is probable, and formal finds what is possible within its assumptions. The example is the ld/en/d counter whose load-priority bug lives in one situation (count 7, ld and en together, d not 0). An over-constrained assumption such as !(ld && en) hides the bug.
needs.interaction: Method explorer on one 8x4 grid: count 0-7 across; hold, increment, load, and load+increment down. A d control slices the third dimension and shows the bug is invisible at d=0. The Directed tab toggles the lesson's three tests and lets the learner build a fourth step list, for example reset, load 7, then ld+en with d=3. Visited cells light up, and the learner predicts found or missed first. The Random tab has controls for P(en), P(ld), the cycle budget (20/100/1000) and the seed. The learner first predicts 'found within 20 cycles?'. Then they see each cell's long-run share (5.6% in the hold and increment rows, 0.6% in the load rows) and the exact probability of reaching the bug from reset within N cycles. Use a Markov chain over count, not a geometric approximation. I checked it: 7.7% at 20 cycles, 40% at 100 and 99.56% at 1,000, which matches the lesson's ~8% and ~99.6%. A seeded run is drawn on top (createRng from coverage-model). The Formal tab toggles the assumption !(ld && en) and asks for a predicted proof result. It then shows the shortest counterexample from a BFS (3 edges: reset, load 7, then ld+en with d≠0) as a CycleWaveform. With the assumption on, the row is greyed and the result reads 'proof passes, bug hidden'. A 'cover property (ld && en): unreachable under assumptions' warning teaches the guard at L686. Fidelity: a deterministic educational model. Formal here is exhaustive reachability, not a tool run; bounded or inconclusive results stay 'tool-dependent'. New pure model src/lib/verification-methods-model.ts; the lesson figure becomes model-generated so its numbers cannot drift.

needs.where: ### Coverage: measuring what you exercised, L403-451 (the hand-traced coverage report code block L421-438 and its explanation L439-440)
needs.concept: Code coverage counts what code ran; functional coverage counts the planned scenarios. Neither checks anything. 100% statement and branch coverage can coexist with a plan hole (reset mid-count) and with a disabled compare. This is misconception #1 on the spine card.
needs.interaction: 'What did this run cover?' The up_counter RTL is annotated with live per-line hit counts (always_ff 20, rst 1, wrap 2, increment 17, as in the lesson's trace). It also shows branch true/false and toggle per bit, where §40.2.2 counts a bit as toggled once it is seen at 0 and at 1. Beside it are the plan's functional items: reset to 0, increment, wrap 7->0, reset mid-count, checks with !==. The learner can add 'assert rst at cycle k', change the run length (5, 9 or 20 cycles) or disable the compare. Predict before each run: (1) adding a mid-count reset changes statement and branch coverage? No, the reset at the first edge already covered that branch. (2) Does functional coverage change? Yes, reset mid-count goes from 0 to 1. (3) With the compare disabled, code and functional coverage stay at 100% while checks = 0, and the verdict reads 'no evidence'. A 5-cycle run never takes the wrap branch, which separates branch coverage from statement coverage. Label branch and condition coverage as tool-defined, since only statement, toggle and FSM are defined in §40.2.2. Keep the lesson's note that some tools count transitions for toggle. Reuse counter-bench-model from the mutation lab.

needs.where: ### The coverage closure trap, L453-503 (static SVG curve L459-495 and the four trap bullets and guards L497-503)
needs.concept: Closure has diminishing returns: one rare bin dominates the sample count, while a targeted directed test or formal closes it at once. Coverage counts as evidence only when its checks were live. A waiver is a decision with a reason, not a fix. 100% of an incomplete coverage model is a false closure.
needs.interaction: Closure budget lab. Controls: the number of common bins (default 16), the rare-bin probability (0.1%, 1% or 5%) and the sample budget. The learner first predicts the samples needed to hit all 17 bins: about 100, 1,000 or 100,000. The reveal shows the expected-coverage curve on a log axis, (1/17)Σ(1-(1-p_i)^n), and the expected samples to close. I checked these: ≈54 for the 16 common bins, ≈1,002 for all 17, and 44.8/68.3/90.7/94.5/97.8/99.96% at 10/20/50/100/1000/5000 samples, all matching the lesson's figure. Compute them with coverage-model harmonic/expectedSamplesDisjoint and overlay a seeded run. Action buttons: 'More seeds' (the plateau barely moves); 'Directed test for the rare bin' (closes it in one run); 'Waive the hole' (needs a reason, and the bin turns striped 'waived', not 'covered'); 'Checks were off in these runs' (the coverage bar stays while a separate 'evidence' bar drops to 0); 'The plan has 2 items the model lacks' (the denominator grows and 100% drops). The concept map lists 'Closure loop with a budget' as missing (P1c), so this fills a tracked gap.
needs.existing: CoverageCrossExplorerVisualizer mode="closure"
needs.gap: It is an addr x op covergroup cross that shows covergroup, dist and std::randomize source; covergroup syntax belongs to I-SV-3A and is out of scope for F1B. It has no simple 'N common bins + 1 rare bin' preset, no coverage-against-samples curve with a budget, and no toggles for the trap cases (checks off, waivers, incomplete model). needs.concept: A packed struct is one vector: the first member is the most significant, and the struct can be sliced, compared and printed with %h (§7.2.1). An unpacked struct has no bit numbering. needs.concept: Hard vs soft packed unions. Every member names the same bits, and writing one member then reading another is defined and independent of host byte order (§7.3.1). Hard packed requires equal widths, otherwise it is an error. Soft packed (new in 1800-2023) is as wide as its widest member, right-justifies every member, and leaves the bits above the written member unaffected (§7.3.1). The union as a whole is a vector, unsigned by default.

Predict gate for word_u: after w.word = 32'hAAAA_BBBB; w.half = 16'h1234, choose AAAA_1234, 1234_BBBB (placed at the MSB like a struct) or 0000_1234 (assumed the upper bits clear); the reveal keeps AAAA dashed and labelled 'unaffected'. needs.concept: The three levels of type compatibility. Matching (§6.22.1): an anonymous type matches only within one statement; each module instance gets its own local type; a package typedef matches everywhere it is imported. Equivalent (§6.22.2): packed types with the same bit count, 2/4-state and signedness are equivalent, so struct packed signed {bit [3:0] a, b;} is equivalent to byte. Assignment compatible (§6.22.3): all integral types. This is why unpacked structs fail across modules while packed ones assign.

needs.where: ### The conditional operator and x merging (lines 508-524)
needs.concept: With an x or z condition, ?: evaluates both branches. If they are logically equal it returns that value; otherwise it merges them bit by bit with Table 11-20, where z merged with anything gives x (§11.4.11). For the same condition, if/else takes the else branch (§12.4) and hides the unknown. This is X-optimism vs X-pessimism, which the spine card requires.

needs.where: ### Streaming operators (lines 400-467, especially the target rules at 455-458); Push Further 'Streaming aggregates and byte order at scale' (lines 750-755)
needs.concept: Streaming in three steps: pack (operands left first, struct members in declaration order, queue element 0 first, §11.4.14.1); slice from the right and reverse the slice order (§11.4.14.2); fit into the target. A wider fixed target is left-aligned and zero-filled on the right, a narrower one is an error, and a queue or dynamic target is resized. Unpack consumes from the MSB end, and too few bits is an error (§11.4.14.3). Whole-struct {<< byte} also swaps the field order. with [0 +: hdr.len] limits a variable field, and greedy resizing applies without it (§11.4.14.4).
needs.interaction: Struct fields len/addr/kind are drawn as coloured segments. Choose {>> {hdr}}, {<< 8 {hdr}} or {<< {hdr}} and a target (32-bit, 40-bit, 24-bit, byte queue). PREDICT q[0], the target value, or 'error'. Then step pack, slice, reverse, fit. Unpack mode fills back from the MSB end. Presets: big-endian into a byte queue, little-endian, 40-bit target zero-filled on the right, 24-bit target error, whole-struct byte reversal vs per-field swap, a variable-length payload with 'with', and a remainder slice ({<< 4 {6'b11_0101}}, the LRM's own example).

needs.where: ### Concatenation and replication (lines 344-375)
needs.concept: Concatenation members are self-determined and joined MSB first, and the result is unsigned. Replication repeats with a constant count. Unsized constants are illegal inside braces. A concatenation can be an assignment target, a replication cannot (§11.4.12, §11.4.12.1).
needs.interaction: PREDICT {a, b} and {2{a}} for edited operands, then try {a, 1} and read the compile error with its clause.
needs.existing: OperatorExplorer family="concat" (the family exists in operatorCatalog: {a, b}, {2{a}}, and the {a, 1} unsized trap; embedded by no lesson)
needs.gap: The concat family has no concatenation-as-target ({hi, lo} = 16'hBEEF), no hand sign-extension preset ({{4{n[3]}}, n}), and the replication count is fixed at 2. These are small catalog additions. The family is usable as it is.

needs.where: ### Equality (line 173, operands of different widths) and Push Further line 737 (sig == 1'bx)
needs.concept: Before comparing, the narrower equality operand is zero-extended, or sign-extended when both operands are signed. So a 4-bit sig == 1'bx compares with 4'b000x, and any 1 in sig[3:1] gives a definite 0, not x (§11.4.5).
needs.interaction: Set operand widths independently and PREDICT a == b. The extended operand appears with its added bits marked before the bit-by-bit comparison.
needs.existing: OperatorExplorer family="equality" (embedded at line 187)
needs.gap: BitEditor operand widths are fixed by FAMILY_DEFAULTS, so a width mismatch cannot be explored. Add per-slot width controls, and an initial-inputs or preset prop so a lesson can open on the mismatch.

needs.where: ### Four-state truth (lines 150-152: & for &&, ~ for !)
needs.concept: Bitwise vs logical: 4'b0100 & 4'b0010 is 4'b0000 (false) while && gives 1. ~4'b0001 is 4'b1110 (true) while ! gives 0 (§11.4.7, §11.4.8).
needs.interaction: Compare mode: the same operands under & and && (or ~ and !) side by side. PREDICT the truth value each one gives to an if.
needs.existing: OperatorExplorer (bitwise and logical families, one operator at a time)
needs.gap: There is no two-operator compare view. A static two-column table (see the static additions) is probably enough.

needs.where: Push Further 'Evaluation order, side effects and short-circuits' (lines 757-766)
needs.concept: Only &&, || and -> short-circuit, and ?: evaluates only the chosen branch unless the condition is x/z. Every other operator evaluates all its operands, so ptr_valid & f(ptr) calls f (§11.3.5, §11.4.7, §11.4.11).
needs.interaction: Pick an operator (&&, &, ||, |, ?: with a known or an x condition), set the left operand, PREDICT whether f() runs, then see a call counter and a side-effect log.
needs.gap: This would need a new small model. A static SequenceDiagram (see the static additions) teaches it almost as well.

needs.where: ### Associative arrays: entries only where you write, 'Reads, defaults and allocation' (lines 330-334); also Quiz Q4 and Q12
needs.concept: What each access does to an associative array: a plain read returns the Table 7-1 value with a warning and allocates nothing (§7.8.6). Only an assignment target, a ref actual and a read-modify-write allocate (§7.8.7). A declared '{default: v}' changes what a missing read returns and removes the warning, but not exists()/num() (§7.9.11). exists() never warns (§7.9.3), and delete(k) on a missing key is silent (§7.9.2).
needs.interaction: Pick a statement card (v = aa[k]; aa[k] = v; aa[k]++; aa[k] += 2; pass aa[k] to a ref argument; aa.exists(k); aa.delete(k)). Toggle 'declares default' and element type int vs logic [7:0]. Predict three things: the value returned, whether a warning appears, and num() afterwards. Then the key strip shows whether an entry appears, with the clause. Include the LRM's own example as a preset: int a[int] = '{default:1}; a[1]++ allocates a[1] at 1, then it becomes 2.
needs.existing: DynamicStructureVisualizer initialKind="assoc" (already has read/write/exists/delete-key/num with predictions)
needs.gap: systemverilog-array-model has no declared default on AssocArrayState and no read-modify-write or ref-argument AssocOp; the component has no initial-contents or preset prop. Add a default field, 'rmw' and 'ref-arg' ops with predictions, and an initialPreset prop.

Wrong predictions are diagnosed: insert read as 'after i', pop_back read as the front, pop treated as a peek.

needs.where: ### Queues, slicing predictions (lines 217-242)
needs.concept: Queue index and slice rules (§7.10.1): q[a:b] has b-a+1 items; a > b gives {}; a < 0 is the same as 0; b > $ is the same as $; Q[n:n] outside the range gives {}; an invalid read returns the missing-element value; writing q[$+1] appends; a write outside 0..$+1 is ignored with a required warning.

needs.where: ### Queues, 'A queue never blocks' (lines 255-257)
needs.concept: wait (q.size() > 0) and pop_front() are two separate steps. With two consumers and one item, a legal interleaving (§4.7) lets both pass the wait, and the second pop returns the missing-element value. A mailbox get() waits and removes in one call (§15.4.5).
needs.interaction: A producer lane and consumer lanes A and B, with one item pushed. The learner picks the scheduler's interleaving (marked with a 'Scheduler choice' badge) or steps through it, and predicts what B's pop_front returns. Then the learner switches the shared queue to a mailbox and sees each message go to exactly one get().

needs.where: ### Iterate safely, store safely (lines 632-650) and Push Further, deleting during a first()/next() walk (lines 881-902)
needs.concept: Resizing an array inside its own foreach is undefined (§12.7.3); the safe options are a two-pass cleanup, or a one-pass first()/next() walk, which is defined because next() finds the smallest key greater than its argument even after that key was deleted (§7.9.6).
needs.interaction: int-keyed exp_by_id has keys 1, 4, 9, and 4 and 9 hold empty queues. Pick a strategy (foreach + delete, find_index then delete, first()/next() walk) and step through it. Predict what next(id) returns and where id lands after deleting the current key. The foreach strategy shows an 'undefined (§12.7.3)' panel, not a made-up outcome.

needs.where: ### Expert: Stale references and hidden copies (lines 904-910); also the post-3D note at line 263
needs.concept: Which operations outdate a ref to an element. Queue methods keep references to surviving elements valid, and a ref follows its element even when the element's index changes. Removing that element, assigning the whole queue, new[] or delete() on a dynamic array, assoc delete(k), and a bounded push_front/insert that pushes the element out all outdate it (§7.10.3, §13.5.2, §7.5.1).
needs.interaction: A task holds a ref to one element, drawn as a pinned arrow. Pick an operation, then predict 'still live (at which index?)' or 'outdated'. Then see the arrow follow its element or detach onto a ghost box, and see a write through the ref land in the array or vanish.

needs.where: ### Array query functions (lines 520-545)
needs.concept: $left/$right/$low/$high/$increment/$size per dimension and the dimension numbering of a mixed array (§20.7: the slowest-varying dimension is 1). For bit [31:0] exp_by_id [int][$], dimension 1 is the associative key, 2 the queue and 3 the packed bits. $dimensions is 3, $unpacked_dimensions is 2, and $size(exp_by_id, 2) is illegal (§20.7.1). On an int-keyed associative array, $right is the largest possible index, not the largest key.
needs.interaction: Pick an array (int f[7:0], a queue of 3, an empty queue, an assoc with keys 5 and 9, an empty assoc, the tracker array) and a dimension, predict each query value, then reveal. In 3D the sparse key axis (gaps between keys), the per-key queue rows of different lengths and the 32-bit packed depth are three axes. Clicking an axis selects that dimension number and shows its readout or the illegal-dimension error.

(no: UNEXPECTED), then pop_front and compare, then delete the key if empty. final raises an error per pending ID and prints the summary. Reveal it step by step in sync with the trace table.

The same structures inside UVM, lines 940-944: a comparison table of native associative array vs uvm_pool. Missing-key read: native returns the default with a warning and allocates nothing (§7.8.6); uvm_pool::get allocates (IEEE 1800.2-2020 §11.2.2.4; verified in uvm-core 2020.3.1 uvm_pool.svh). Delete of a missing key: native is silent (§7.9.2); uvm_pool::delete issues a POOLDEL warning (uvm-core 2020.3.1). needs.concept: The time-0 reset race. All initial/always procedures start at time 0 in no promised order (§9.2). A blocking rst_n = 0 can run before always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) reaches its event control, so the x->0 negedge (Table 9-2) is missed. With rst_n <= 0 the update lands in NBA, after every time-0 procedure has run to its first timing control (§4.5, §10.4.2). A declaration initializer is applied before any procedure starts and is never an event (§6.8).
needs.interaction: A toggle inside the code line picks the reset style: rst_n = 1'b0 in an initial, rst_n <= 1'b0, or logic rst_n = 1'b0 in the declaration. Blocking: flop first resets at 0; bench first leaves state x until the 5 ns posedge, where rst_n is low. NBA: resets at 0 in every order. Initializer: never an event, so state is x until 5 ns. The narration cites the Table 9-2 x->0 cell.

needs.concept: Which value changes are events. These are posedge/negedge per Table 9-2 (x->0 and z->0 are negedge, 0->z is posedge), and 'edge' means either one. Edge events look at the LSB only, and an operand change that leaves the expression's value unchanged is no event (§9.4.2). @(a or b) is the same as @(a, b) (§9.4.2.1). In @(a iff en) the guard is evaluated when a changes, not when en changes, and must be true per §12.4, so x/z is false. iff binds tighter than or (§9.4.2.3).
needs.interaction: Edge-detector drill. The learner sets a signal's old and new value (0/1/x/z), or a 4-bit bus old/new value, and optionally a guard en. Before the reveal they tick which of @(posedge s), @(negedge s), @(edge s), @(s) and @(posedge s iff en) would wake. The reveal lights the matching Table 9-2 cell and states the governing rule. Presets: 'x->0 active-low reset', '1->z', 'bus 4'b0011->4'b0010 (LSB 1->0: negedge)', 'bus 4'b0001->4'b0011 (LSB unchanged: @(bus) wakes, @(posedge bus) does not)', '@(a & b) where b changes but a & b does not', 'en = x in the iff guard', 'iff binds tighter than or'.

needs.concept: Deferred violation reports. The check runs when the statement executes, but the report waits in that process's queue until the Observed region. A flush point discards it: the procedure resumes after an event control or wait, or an always_comb/always_latch is re-triggered by an input. A report that has matured can no longer be flushed. needs.where: ### Feeding a test from files (lines 387-427); Debug it cases 2 and 3 (lines 811-853); ### Expert: Robust vector parsing (lines 916-922)
needs.concept:
The read-call contract on a character stream:
- $fopen returns 0 on failure (§21.3.1).
- $fscanf skips white space, newlines included, and returns the number of items assigned (§21.3.4.3).
- It returns 0 on an early mismatch and leaves the offending character unread.
- It returns -1 (EOF) only when the input ends before the first conversion, and then assigns nothing.
- It leaves trailing white space, including the final newline, unread.
- $feof is nonzero only after a read has already hit the end (§21.3.8).
- With %h %h %h, a short line silently takes its missing field from the next line.
- $fgets plus $sscanf per line avoids that (§21.3.4.2).
This is the core skill of the page and the root of two of the four 'log that lies' bugs.

Severity tasks report; they do not decide pass or fail:
- $info, $warning and $error print and return, so the run continues and no counter changes.
- $fatal(n) prints and calls $finish(n), and final blocks then run in zero time.
- $stop only suspends the run, so final blocks do not run at that point.
- The PASS/FAIL line comes only from the bench's own counters.

needs.where: ### When does it print?: the $monitor trace (lines 212-244); Debug it case 1 (lines 794-809); Expert $fmonitor bullet (line 878)
needs.concept:
$monitor watch semantics:
- Only one list is active at a time.
- It prints at the end of each time slot in which a listed argument changed.
- Several changes in one slot give one line, with the final values.
- Changes of $time, $stime and $realtime do not count.
- A new call silently replaces the list.
- $monitoroff pauses it; $monitoron resumes it and prints at once.
- Any number of $fmonitor lists can run side by side.

Sources: §21.2.3, §21.3.2.

Setup:

- Lanes for a and b.
- The active watch list drawn as a band that changes when a new $monitor call runs.

Predict:
- For each slot: prints or silent, and the exact line.

Controls:
- Move or delete the second $monitor call.
- Add b to the first list.
- Insert $monitoroff or $monitoron at a chosen time.
- Switch to $fmonitor, so that two lists stay active.

Observe:
- Postponed print markers.
- One collapsed line for the double change at 20 ns.
- Silence at 30 ns, because b is not watched and $time does not count.

needs.where: ### Printing: $display, $write and format specifiers (lines 86-145); quiz question 2
needs.concept:
How a printed number is sized and how unknown bits print:
- The field width comes from the largest value the expression can hold.
- Decimal is padded with spaces; hex, octal and binary keep their leading zeros.
- %0 prints the minimum width.
- Each hex or octal digit group follows the x/X/z/Z rules, and so does a decimal value.
- %b prints every bit.

Sources: §21.2.1.2, §21.2.1.3.
needs.interaction:
Setup:

- Toggle each bit through 0, 1, x and z.
- Choose %d, %0d, %h, %0h, %o or %b.

Predict:
- The exact text, in a row of character cells with spaces visible as a dot.

Observe:
- 4-bit or 3-bit group brackets over the bit strip.
- Each group mapped to its character, with the rule that fired: all x gives x, some x gives X, z gives Z unless an x is present.
- The width calculation: for 12 bits, 4095 needs 4 decimal columns and FFF needs 3 hex columns.

Presets:
- r1 = 10 on 12 bits, the lesson's padding line.
- 4'b10x1.
- All z.
- x and z in one digit.

needs.where: ### Printing time: $time, $realtime, %t and $timeformat (lines 344-385); quiz question 8; reusable in F3A (spine objective: predict $time, $stime and $realtime, and format them with $timeformat)
needs.concept:
How a time value reaches the log:
- $time is rounded to the calling module's time unit; $realtime keeps the fraction.
- %t converts to the $timeformat unit.
- By default that unit is the smallest precision of any `timescale in the design, with no fraction, no suffix and a width of 20.
- $timeformat(units, precision, suffix, min_width) changes every %t until the next call.

Sources: §20.3, §20.4.3, Tables 20-2 and 20-3.

Predict:

Observe:

needs.where: ### Configuring a run from the command line: plusargs (lines 475-510); ### Expert: Plusargs at regression scale (lines 924-931); interview angle 2; quiz question 6
needs.concept:
How plusarg lookups match:
- Matching is by prefix.
- Plusargs are searched in command-line order, so the first match wins.
- A miss returns 0, leaves the variable unchanged and warns nobody.
- On a match, the remainder is converted with the format; an empty remainder stores zero or an empty string.
- Characters the format cannot convert write 'bx, so a 4-state variable reads X while an int silently becomes 0.

Source: §21.6.
needs.interaction:

  - +SEED=12x
  - +SEED=
- The code panel lists the lookups: $test$plusargs("V"), "TEST" versus "TEST=%d", $value$plusargs("SEED=%d", seed).
- A variable-type toggle switches between int and logic [31:0].

Predict:
- Each return value and the resulting variable value.

Observe:

- The matched prefix and the remainder are highlighted.
- The conversion result appears in a ValueChip.

needs.where: ### Loading memories: $readmemh (lines 429-473); Kata 2; quiz question 7
needs.concept:
Where $readmemh puts each number:
- By default the load pointer starts at the lowest address and moves upward.
- With only a start address it moves upward from there.
- With start greater than finish it moves downward, and that direction holds even after an @ line.
- @ addresses are hexadecimal, so @10 means address 16; the page never says this.
- Cells the file never reaches keep their old value, which is X for logic.
- Sized or based numbers are not allowed.
- When the task gives an address range, an @ address outside it is an error that ends the load.
- With start and finish given and no @ lines, a word-count mismatch is a warning.

Source: §21.4.
needs.interaction:
Setup:
- The memory is drawn as an address column of 16 rows (or 32 for the @10 preset).
- The file pane is filled from presets: the lesson's rom.hex, @4 aa bb, @10, a short file, 8'h12, @ outside the range.
- The start and finish arguments can be set.

Predict:
- Click cells to say which values land where.

Observe:
- Step the pointer one token at a time.
- Unwritten cells are hatched X.
- Each warning or error carries its clause.

Why not 3D: this is a one-dimensional unpacked array, so depth would add nothing.

Build: new src/lib/sv-readmem-model.ts, or a readmem operation in systemverilog-array-model.

needs.where: ### Random numbers without classes: $urandom and $urandom_range (lines 512-530)
needs.concept:
Why $random % 10 can be negative and $urandom_range(9) cannot:
- $random returns a signed 32-bit value (§20.14.1).

needs.where: ### The scheduler loop: how time advances (lines 77-163), plus 'What you just saw' (lines 60-76)
needs.concept: Time advances only when the current time slot is empty: the simulator jumps to the earliest booked time (§4.4, §4.5), only delays book later slots, and a run ends in one of four ways: nothing left booked (§9.6.1), $finish (§20.2), never (a free-running clock with no $finish), or a hang with time stopped (zero-delay loop, §9.2.2.1).
needs.interaction: Step a small program while the §4.5 loop flowchart lights the box being executed. Two lists update with each step: 'this time slot' (◆ update / ▶ evaluation events) and 'booked for later', sorted by due time, which is the lesson's to-do-list analogy made visible. Before every jump the learner predicts the next time visited, and before the end predicts how and when the run ends. Variant picker: $finish at 22 ns; a blocked waiter with nothing booked (ends quietly); a free-running clock with no $finish (still running at the horizon); always areg = ~areg; (time stops).

needs.where: ### Time units and precision: the rounding table and the 'One delay, two modules' figure (lines 300-379); also Expert: delay values that are not what they look like (lines 700-705)
needs.concept: The time unit scales #d and the element's own precision rounds it (§3.14, §3.14.1). A finer precision elsewhere does not help. A time literal is converted to the current unit (§5.8) and then rounded. §3.14.1 sets no rule for halfway ties. Delays of x or z count as 0, and a negative delay becomes a huge unsigned value (§9.4.1).
needs.interaction: Pick a unit and a precision (1, 10 or 100 of s through fs; a precision coarser than the unit is rejected, §3.14), type #d or a time literal such as #2.1ns, and predict the wake time. The reveal is a ruler of precision ticks with the scaled delay snapping to the nearest tick. Presets: the six table rows; #1.55 at 1ns/100ps (the spine's assessment item); #2.1ns at 10ns/1ns; #0.4 at 1ns/1ns (runs in the same slot); #2.85 at 1ns/100ps, shown as tool-dependent because round-half-up and round-half-even disagree; #(x) and #(-1). A two-module mode puts tb_top (1ns/100ps) and u_slow (10ns/1ns) on one absolute axis, turning the static figure into a live one.

needs.where: ### Reading the time: $time, $stime, $realtime and %t (lines 400-462); the Make It Work predictions (lines 573-604); quiz items at lines 818-838
needs.concept: $time, $stime and $realtime all report in the calling module's time unit, not the precision. $time rounds to an integer, $realtime keeps the fraction, and $stime returns the low 32 bits (§20.3.1-§20.3.3). %t converts to the $timeformat units, and the defaults come from Table 20-3 (§20.4.3).

The reveal is three aligned rulers: absolute time, the caller's units, and the integer that $time rounds to. Set $timeformat (units_number -15 to 2 from Table 20-2, fractional digits, suffix, minimum width), or choose 'no call' to see the Table 20-3 default, which is tool-dependent when the build has only timeunit and no `timescale. Toggle %t of $time vs $realtime to watch the fraction disappear. Presets: the §20.3.1 experiment (2 and 1.6, then 3 and 3.2), the Make It Work two-module bench, and the UVM '@ 15000' stamp.

needs.where: 'Which unit applies?' (lines 381-388), Expert: which time unit applies (lines 674-684), and the quiz item at line 862
needs.concept: An element with no timeunit takes its unit from the first rule that applies: the enclosing module if nested, else the last `timescale earlier in the compilation unit, else a compilation-unit timeunit, else the implementation default (§3.14.2.3). A `timescale reaches later files of the same compilation unit (§3.14.2.1), and how files map to compilation units is tool-specific (§3.12.1). `resetall cuts the reach (§22.3). Mixing elements that declare a unit with elements that do not is an error (§3.14.2.3).
needs.interaction: The learner reorders a file list with Move up / Move down buttons: a.sv with `timescale 1ns/1ps, b.sv with no unit, c.sv with timeunit 100ps, a package with no unit, an optional `resetall, an optional compilation-unit timeunit and a nested module. A switch chooses 'one compilation unit' or 'each file its own'. The learner predicts b's unit, then sees every element tagged with its resolved unit and precision, the precedence rule (a-d) that decided it, any mixed-specification error, and the resulting global precision.
needs.gap: Needs a resolver in the timescale model, for example resolveTimescales(files, order, cuMode). The tool default must be shown as 'implementation-specific', never as a number, and whether the mixed case is reported as an error or a warning must be labelled tool-dependent.

needs.where: Expert: time values that cross scopes (lines 692-699) and ### Debug challenge: the 1000x delay (lines 911-958)
needs.concept: A time literal is converted where it is written (§5.8). time, realtime and int values carry no unit, so the callee reads the number in its own unit. Converting a real to a time value rounds, with halves away from zero (§6.12.1). Fixes: scale inside the callee with #(delay_ns * 1ns), agree one project unit, or pass clock-cycle counts.

needs.where: ### The order the standard leaves open: the time-0 race (lines 239-287)
needs.concept: The standard sets no order between initial and always procedures at time 0 (§9.2) or among processes woken together (§4.3, §4.7), so one bench can legally print 3 lines or 2. A declaration initializer runs before any process starts (§6.8) and removes the race.

The model runs every legal order and shows the grouped outcomes side by side from the first step where they diverge: Order A (the always block is already waiting, 3 lines) and Order B (2 lines). Toggling between 'logic a = 0;' (initializer) and 'a = 0;' inside the initial block collapses the outcomes into one deterministic group.

needs.where: ### Processes, events and time slots: the 'What wakes a process' table and 'Only a real change counts' (lines 41-55)
needs.concept: @(expr) wakes only on a change that happens while it waits. posedge and negedge include x transitions (Table 9-2: x->0 is a negedge). wait(expr) passes at once if the level is already true (§9.4.3). Rewriting the same value wakes nothing, and @(a & b) wakes only when the result changes (§9.4.2).
needs.interaction: Pick a waiter (@(a), @(posedge a), @(negedge a), @(a & b) or wait (a)) and step a script of writes (a: x->0, 0->0, 0->1; b: 0->1). Before each write the learner predicts 'wakes' or 'stays asleep', then sees the waiter's lane and the rule that decided.

needs.where: 'The global precision and 1step' (line 390) and Expert: global precision and 1step (lines 685-691)
needs.concept: The global precision is the minimum over every timeprecision, every precision written with timeunit, and the smallest `timescale precision, even one that every element overrides. 1step equals it, and $printtimescale($root) prints it as both unit and precision (§3.14.3, §20.4.2).

needs.where: ### Overriding rules: what must match (lines 246-257) + Push Further ### Expert: override specifiers :initial, :extends, :final (lines 512-541)
needs.concept: Which override prototypes are legal (§8.20). Matching argument types, identical names, qualifiers and directions. A covariant return type is allowed (§8.20 Example 2: a typedef of int matches int, logic does not). Defaults must be present in both or neither, but their values may differ. Static methods cannot be virtual (§8.10), constructors cannot be virtual (§8.7). Specifier rules: :initial (no virtual override, does not imply virtual), :extends (must override a virtual, implies virtual), :final (no later override, illegal on pure virtual), :initial and :extends mutually exclusive, an extern body repeats no specifiers.

Before running, the learner predicts the class of q, the $cast(back, q) result, id, crc, same_hdr, or a null access. Then they step a call-trace lane view (tb_top, orig, c, header@2) synchronized with the heap view. Presets: correct, clone not virtual, no override, no super.copy, unchecked cast with a plain rhs.

needs.where: ### Which declarations are the same type? (lines 171-187), also feeding ### Declaring specializations (130-151) and ### The default specialization (153-169)
needs.concept: A generic class is not a type. Each specialization is the parameter tuple left after defaults are filled in, so fifo, fifo#(), fifo#(int), fifo#(.D(4)) and fifo#(int, 2+2) are one type. fifo#(integer), fifo#(bit [31:0]) and fifo#(byte, 8) are different types, while fifo#(bit signed [31:0]) and fifo#(byte_t) match.
needs.interaction: A 2D 'specialization grid': rows are T values (int, integer, bit [31:0], bit signed [31:0], byte, byte_t, string) and columns are D values (2, 4, 8, 16). The learner picks a declaration from a palette or builds one (positional, named, partial, #(), bare name, typedef), predicts which existing cell it lands in or whether it creates a new cell, then commits. The reveal shows the canonical (T, D) tuple, which parameters took their defaults, and the rule for each parameter: §8.25 rule a or b, §6.22.1 rule b (typedef rename) or rule e (2-state/4-state, signedness, width, range [w-1:0]). Illegal forms give a compile verdict instead of a cell: fifo #(4, string) (positional order), D d; when p has no default (§8.25), and a named override of a parameter declared in the class body (a local parameter, §6.20.4 / A.10 note 7). Presets: 'same-type' (the seven table rows), 'declaring' (f1-f7), 'no-default', 'local-param', and an advanced set (anonymous struct written twice, untyped C#(4) vs C#(4'd4) per §6.20.2, byte vs bit signed [7:0], logic signed [31:0] vs integer). needs.where: ### Abstract classes and pure virtual methods (lines 272-366), including 'The pattern to notice' and 'Pure virtual versus an empty body'
needs.concept: A virtual class cannot be constructed, and its constructor runs only through super.new from a complete subclass. A subclass is complete only when every pure virtual method has a body with the identical signature. An empty-bodied virtual method is not pure: it is callable and returns the return variable's initial value (§8.21 NOTE), so a forgotten override compiles and silently returns 0. The non-virtual run() calling the virtual check() dispatches to the object's class.
needs.interaction: A construct-it lab. Toggles: base declared 'virtual class' or 'class'; base check() is pure virtual, a virtual with an empty body, or a virtual with a body; range_check implements check(int value), omits it, or declares check(int value, int limit). Then the learner picks an action (new base_check, new range_check, chk = rc; chk.run(7); chk.run(42)) and predicts: compile error, or the output lines and failure count. The reveal gives the verdict with its clause: abstract construction (§8.21), incomplete subclass (§8.21), signature mismatch (§8.20), empty body so both values FAIL and failures=2 (§8.21 NOTE), and a pure method in a plain class marked tool-dependent (§8.20 Example 3). A call trace run() then check() shows which body runs. It also covers the quiz item where a non-virtual report() redeclared in the subclass is invisible through a base handle (§8.14).

needs.where: ### Reaching members with :: (lines 258-270) and Push Further ### Expert: names inside a parameterized class (lines 599-603)
needs.concept: What the :: prefix means depends on where it is written. Outside the class, C::x is illegal and C#()::x, C#(3)::x or a typedef is required. Inside C or its out-of-block methods, C::x names the current specialization. A bare C that is not before :: always means the default specialization, even inside C (the node next; linked-list trap). A type parameter cannot be reached through a handle, and bf.D through a handle is legal but not a constant expression.
needs.interaction: Pick where the code is written (module, inside C's body, out-of-block method, another class) and the form (C::x, C#()::x, C#(3)::x, typedef_t::x, a declaration 'C next;', bf.T, bf.D used as an array size). Predict 'legal or illegal, and which specialization?', then reveal with §8.25, §8.25.1 and §8.5, highlighting the cell it reaches on the specialization grid. Preset 'linked-list' walks node #(type T = int) used as node #(string).

needs.where: Push Further ### Expert: where a class is declared decides how many types exist (lines 593-597) and Kata 2 step 5 (lines 952, 961)
needs.concept: Where the generic class is declared decides how many types exist. In a package, all matching specializations are one type. A module instantiated N times creates N generic classes, so the two instances' fifo#(int) are different types. The same file `included into two packages gives two unrelated classes with the same name, so assignment and $cast fail.
needs.interaction: Choose the declaration site (package, module instantiated 1 to 3 times, `include into two packages) and predict how many distinct fifo#(int) types exist and whether 'a = b' compiles across them. The reveal draws one plane per generic class, each holding its own specialization grid and statics, and marks cross-plane assignments as errors (§8.25, §6.22.1 rule d, §26.2). 2D small multiples work at 390 px. A 3D stack of planes is defensible because the third axis (which generic class) has meaning, but it adds little over side-by-side planes.

needs.where: ### randc: one permutation per object (lines 144-179) and ### Expert: randc state, copies and static variables (lines 569-574)
needs.concept: randc is random-cyclic per object (§18.4.2). Each object has its own permutation. A cycle never repeats inside itself, but a value may repeat across the boundary. The permutation is recomputed when the constraints on the variable change or no remaining value satisfies them. static randc shares one sequence across instances. A shallow copy (new p1) copies the cyclic state (§8.12). A new UVM item per transaction starts a fresh cycle each time. This is spine misconception 4.

Before each call the learner ticks every value the call could return. The reveal shows the set the rules guarantee, one seeded draw labelled 'one possible run', and the clause that decides it (for example, after 2, 0, 3 the only possible 4th value is 1; on a fresh object any value is possible; a copy p2 continues a's cycle). Expert preset: copy and static. Show only what the LRM guarantees: after a constraint change, say that the cycle restarts and the next value may be any value satisfying the current constraints, not a tool-specific permutation.

needs.concept: dist both restricts and weights (§18.5.3). := gives the weight to every value of a range and :/ to the range as a whole, while weights are ratios over the total. needs.where: ### soft: a default with a rank (lines 274-322, the is_secure predict and reveal)
needs.concept: soft is a priority, not a probability (§18.5.13). An uncontested soft constraint holds on every call and is dropped as a whole only when it conflicts. Later beats earlier, derived beats base, inline beats class, and every hard constraint beats every soft one (§18.5.13.1). A kept soft default shrinks the legal set like a hard constraint, which is how the is_secure trap starves a branch. This is spine misconception 1.

The dropped-soft status names the rule each time. A second preset should reproduce the is_secure trap. Restrict x to {0,1} (is_secure) and y to 0..3 (burst_len), with soft y == 2 and (x == 1) -> (y == 1). The learner predicts P(x==1) (0%), then switches to the scoped form (x == 0) -> soft y == 2 and sees 50%.

The problem collects the active variables and blocks, including a rand member's constraints (global, §18.5.8) and inline with (§18.7). On success the values are assigned, post_randomize() runs and the call returns 1. On failure it returns 0, the variables keep their previous values and post_randomize() is skipped (§18.6.3). post_randomize() cannot change the current call.

needs.concept: Random stability. Each new() seeds the object's RNG with the next value of the creating thread's RNG (§18.14.1, object stability). Child threads are seeded from the parent (hierarchical seeding). Inserting an object, thread or draw before existing ones shifts every later seed. A thread-RNG draw made after the objects exist does not change their randomize() results (§18.14.3 example). An object that seeds itself with srandom() keeps its stream (§18.13.3).

needs.concept: Hierarchical seeding and random stability (§18.14.1-§18.14.3): each process and each object has its own RNG. new and fork take the next draw from the creating process. Process-level calls ($urandom, $urandom_range, std::randomize, randcase, randsequence, shuffle) advance the process RNG. obj.randomize() advances only that object's RNG. Process order does not matter. Inserting work early shifts everything created after it.

The learner picks one edit from a palette: rerun, x=new() before a, x=new() after b, junk=$urandom between a and s, std::randomize/randcase/randsequence between a and s, extra a.randomize(), swap two existing processes. Before seeing anything, they mark MATCH or DIFF for a, s and b. Weight expressions are evaluated each execution. Each weight is self-determined in width, summed at the widest weight's width, and each summand is unsigned (§18.16).
needs.interaction: New RandcaseWeightLab (model src/lib/randcase-model.ts; could live in the same model file as randsequence). Knob fields hold the three weights (the w_err knob, or the LRM's 3/1/4). The learner enters or picks each branch's probability, then sees a stacked bar of the exact fractions and a seeded 8000-draw histogram. Presets: 'lesson' (3,1,0), 'lrm' (3,1,4), 'all-zero' (shows 'no branch taken, a warning can be issued'; nothing else is asserted), 'narrow-sum' (bit [7:0] a=200, b=100 gives weight a+b = 44 in 8 bits, shown on a bit strip with the discarded carry), 'signed-byte' (byte -1 weighs 255 as an unsigned summand), plus the cast fix int'(a)+int'(b). Do not model evaluation order or draw count, which are unspecified.

needs.where: ### option versus type_option (lines 149-174) and Push Further weights bullets 2 and 5 (lines 305, 308)
needs.concept: Each instance owns its own option copy, while there is one static type_option copy per type. per_instance defaults to 0, so only the type number is guaranteed in the database (spine misconception 4). A reset pulse between edges disables attempts in flight. A flop-driven reset acts at the edge where it changes. disable iff ($sampled(rst)) and an antecedent guard behave differently (misconception 4).

They pick the guard: disable iff (!rst_n), default disable iff, disable iff ($sampled(rst)) or an antecedent guard rst_n && req |-> .... For each attempt in flight they predict disabled, pass or fail. The reveal draws a continuous-time waveform with one disable-window bar per attempt, from Observed of its start edge to its end, and lights the instant the condition became true. A ghost row shows what an edge-only checker would report, for example the false failure at edge 5 in the lesson's figure.

needs.where: ### Watch a simple assertion misfire: the glitch (lines 99-137) and ### Deferred assertions (lines 139-150)
needs.concept: How a deferred report works: the check runs now and its report is queued on the process's own queue with by-value arguments captured. A flush point clears the queue. Per §16.4.2 the only flush points are: resuming from @ or wait, an always_comb/always_latch re-trigger, and disabling the outermost scope. Resuming after #0 is NOT one. A report that survives matures in Observed (#0, call runs in Reactive) or in Postponed (final, call runs there). A simple immediate assertion reports at once.
needs.interaction: Step through the 10 ns time slot of the lesson's glitch bench. The code is generated from model data, with inline controls on each line: switch a1/a2/a3 between assert, assert #0 and assert final, and add or remove the '#0' before b = 1'b1. Predict first: how many reports each assertion prints (0/1/2) and in which region. Then scrub. The RegionLadder sits beside a per-process 'deferred report queue' tray, which shows each entry as pending (dashed amber, with its captured a/b values), flushed (a cross, naming the flush point 'chk resumed from @(a or b)'), matured, or printed. The log tags every line with its region, and the What/Why narration cites §16.4.1 and §16.4.2. Build it as a new DeferredAssertionQueueVisualizer that reuses RegionLadder, CodeTrace, TraceNarration, usePlayback and PredictionPrompt. needs.where: ### Expert: Flow rules for or, and and intersect (L603-611), inside the 664-word stretch
needs.concept: Sibling threads cannot read each other's assignments. After or, a variable flows out only if it flows out of every operand. After and/intersect, a variable flows out if it flows out of at least one operand, unless it is blocked because it is assigned in (and flows out of) both. A variable that does not flow out becomes unassigned (§16.10, precise rules in Annex F.5.4).

PREDICT the outcome: flows out with one value per thread / flows out as the latest assigned value / unassigned / illegal reference. Reveal: two operand lanes that stay separate threads (or) or merge into one (and/intersect), carrying, striking or blanking the x tag. Use the standard's s4/s7/s8 shapes as presets, paraphrased, not copied.

needs.concept: The two tick-selection rules across clocks. `##1` and `|=>` go to the nearest strictly later tick of the new clock. `##0`, `|->` and a multiclocked if/else go to the nearest tick at or after the old tick, which is the same tick only when the new clock ticks in the same time slot (§16.13.1, §16.13.2). Identical clocking-event expressions do not move at all. It also tackles the spine misconception that `##0` delays one cycle: across clocks `##0` may wait, while in a single clock it never does.
needs.interaction: Build new (MulticlockTickVisualizer plus src/lib/sva-multiclock-model.ts). Two clock lanes on a time axis in ns. Presets: the bench's src_clk at 10 ns and dst_clk at 15 ns (coincident every 30 ns); identical expression; same waveform under a different name (`assign clk2 = clk1`), where the multiclock rules still apply; and an unrelated pair where coincidences are rare. The learner picks an operator (|=>, ##1, |->, ##0, if/else) and clicks a source tick where `a` is sampled 1, then predicts by clicking the destination tick they think is checked. PredictionPrompt feedback names each misconception: 'next tick of any clock', 'one full dst cycle later', 'waits for the next coincident edge', '##0 never waits'. The reveal draws the arrow, shades coincident time slots, quotes the strictly-later or at-or-after rule with its clause, and shows a 'compare all operators' row for the chosen tick. The model holds nextTick(clock, t, strict|nonstrict), keys identity on the expression rather than the waveform, and is tested against the lesson's attempts A (50 ns gives 60/60) and B (60 ns gives 75/60) and the quiz cases (90 ns gives 105/90; ##0 at 40 ns gives 45). Keyboard: arrow keys move the selected tick. Reduced motion: draw arrows without animation. 2D because time alignment is one-dimensional, so 3D would add nothing.

A clock flows left to right across linear operators, distributes into the operands of and/or/intersect/if-else/until, and flows into parentheses and named instances but never out of them. Of two juxtaposed clocks only the second counts. No clock flows into disable iff.

needs.where: ### What the standard forbids (lines 222-243) and 'Expert: Semantic leading clocks' (lines 533-539); Quiz Q3, Interview Q2
needs.concept: Multiclock legality. Only ##1 and ##0 may join differently clocked sequences. A maximal singly clocked subsequence may not match empty. The maximal property must have exactly one semantic leading clock, and identity is judged on the expression, not the waveform (`assign clk2 = clk1`). Multiclocked properties are not allowed in a clocking block, nor with a leading clock inferred from an always procedure (§16.13.1, §16.16 rules b, c and e, §16.16.1).

needs.where: ### `default disable iff` and multiclock assertions (lines 245-268), Quiz Q6
needs.concept: default disable iff resolution (§16.15). An explicit clause replaces the default and is never combined with it. A default extends into nested module, interface and program declarations and nested generate blocks, unless those have their own default. It does not extend into instances. Two defaults in one scope are an error. disable iff (1'b0) cancels the default. Two policies for a module that holds a crossing check.
needs.interaction: Build new (a scope-tree resolver, small model). The tree holds a module with a default, a nested module declaration, a generate block with its own default, an instance of another module, and assertions with no clause, their own clause, or disable iff (1'b0). The learner predicts each assertion's effective disable condition, then sees the resolution path highlighted. A Policy 1 / Policy 2 toggle shows which single-domain checks go quiet while the other domain resets, and that Policy 2 without the explicit clause brings back the false alarm.

needs.where: ### Why one clock is not enough (lines 31-41)
needs.concept: A short source-domain pulse can fall between destination ticks, so a dst_clk-only assertion never starts an attempt for it. A src_clk-only assertion cannot count a window in destination ticks.
needs.interaction: A 'sampling' mode of the MulticlockTickVisualizer. The learner drags the start and end of a pulse on the time axis and predicts which src_clk and dst_clk ticks sample it as 1 (Preponed values). The reveal marks each tick's sampled value and whether a dst_clk-clocked assertion would start an attempt. Preset: the lesson's pulse from 60+ to 70+ ns, seen by src 70 and missed by dst 60 and 75.

needs.where: ### Sequence end points across clocks: `.matched` (lines 270-289) and 'Expert: .matched and .triggered at the edges of their rules' (lines 547-552)
needs.concept: `.matched` holds a source sequence's end point from the Observed region of the match until the Observed region after the first destination tick after it. `.triggered` lasts only the rest of that time step. Several source matches before one destination tick fork the evaluation. An empty match sets neither (§16.13.5, §16.13.6).
needs.interaction: An 'end points' mode on the same two lanes. The learner places source end points and can gate the destination clock, predicts the destination tick at which s_burst_done.matched is seen and whether .triggered would be visible there, then sees the held status drawn as a bar from the match to the consuming tick.

staticVisuals: Quick Take, after the analogy bullet (line 18): a one-glance four-tile strip (VisualRecap-style or ArchitectureDiagram). Bell = named event, slotted in-tray = bounded mailbox, key cabinet = semaphore, staff list = process handle. Each tile carries a 'where it breaks' tag: a bell with no listener is lost and .triggered lasts only until time moves; keys carry no names; kill() returns nothing. This splits the ~440-word opening.

After the process method table (line 194): a process state chart drawn with ArchitectureDiagram, every edge labelled with a verb. 'handle null (before self())' leads to RUNNING. RUNNING and WAITING switch on entering and leaving a blocking statement. RUNNING or WAITING goes to SUSPENDED by suspend(), and resume() goes back. A process goes to FINISHED when it ends normally and to KILLED by kill() or disable. Note that kill() on FINISHED or KILLED still kills live descendants, and that await() on self is an error (all from §9.7).

Pitfalls and Debugging (lines 240-248): turn the five pitfalls into a symptom, cause, fix table. Rows: null-handle access at p.kill(); 'does not compile' for process p = process::self() in an initial block (§6.21); keys never back after a timeout; FINISHED read instead of KILLED (the §9.7 race); await() on self; disable fork killing siblings. This breaks the ~415-word stretch.

Mutual exclusion: new(2) breaks it, so it is rejected (two owners at once). Hold and wait: release before you wait, or take everything with one get(n) (§15.3.3). No preemption: release and retry with try_get, which can livelock without a random back-off. Circular wait: one global lock order. Cite Coffman et al. 1971 as general theory.

The timer returns at budget_ns, join_any returns, and disable fork kills the blocked get inside the wrapper. A function may not suspend its own process.

Push Further, a deadlocked bench can end quietly (585-590): a two-column comparison. Left: no clock and no watchdog, so the run ends at the time of the last activity with no message (§9.6.1). Who gets the key next (lines 345-352, reused at lines 743-751): a 'guaranteed vs left open' table. Guaranteed: waiters keep arrival order (§15.3.3). Diagnosing a hang (line 471): a one-glance 'four bug shapes' summary visual that also serves as the lesson's summary picture. Leaked key: an arrow from the semaphore to a finished holder. Lock-order deadlock: a closed cycle. Starvation: one lane always waiting while the others alternate. Surplus key: two holders inside a one-key section. Each shape carries its log symptom and its fix.

Quiet end or hang (line 485): two mini timelines. With no clock and no watchdog the run ends at its last activity with no error (§9.6.1). With a watchdog it ends in $fatal at 1000 ns. In UVM it ends at the global timeout (link to I-UVM-1C).

Make It Work (line 680, the 45 ns row): a SequenceDiagram of the one time slot. A put(1) on bus_lock, then B is granted, B is refused (NACK), B releases the bus, B calls credits.put(1), A receives the credit, A gets bus_lock. This makes the causal order inside a single time slot visible.

Keys survive a kill (lines 760-767): a SequenceDiagram of the uvm-core 2020.3.1 uvm_reg pattern. An access calls XatomicX(1): an owner check, a KILLED holder giving the UVM/REG/ZOMBIE error, then m_atomic.get(1) and m_process = self. reset() calls void'(m_atomic.try_get(1)), then m_atomic.put(1), then m_process = null. Label it as an implementation detail, not IEEE 1800.2-2020. Add a two-lane picture of the two restore patterns.

Ownership and re-entry (lines 769-813): a state diagram for owned_lock. Free -> Held(P, depth 0) on lock() by P; depth + 1 on re-entry by P; $error on unlock() by a non-owner or when the holder has ended; the last unlock() clamps with try_get(1) then put(1) and returns to Free.

Semaphore or sequencer lock (lines 500-504 and 823-825): a decision table. Exclusive use of one agent's driver -> sequencer lock()/grab() (IEEE 1800.2-2020 §14.2.5.5, §14.2.5.6). A resource shared across threads or agents that no sequencer owns -> semaphore. Passing data -> mailbox. 'It happened now' -> event. A chosen order of service -> an arbiter process.

needs.where: ### Text macros: what the compiler actually sees (lines 90-131) and #### Every form of `define (133-174)
needs.concept: A macro substitutes text, not values (§22.5.1). The learner traces formal-to-actual binding, defaults, `" stringify, `` token pasting, and inner macros expanded after the outer one at the point of use. The expanded text is then parsed with normal precedence, and the conditional operator evaluates only the branch it selects (§11.4.11). This is the source of missing-parenthesis, double-evaluation and semicolon bugs.
needs.interaction: A MacroExpansionLab with presets: SQ bare, SQ parenthesized, MAX(bump(),0), MAX(bump(),20) with cnt=10, TB_CLK_PERIOD with a trailing ';', TB_LOG_BLOCK followed by ';' and an else, TB_SHOW vs TB_SHOW0, TB_REG pasting, TB_QUOTE, MACRO1 defaults including the illegal `MACRO1(1), and the LRM's own TOP(TOP(b,1),TOP(42,a)). Error presets cover too many arguments, a missing argument with no default, a missing '()' and a recursive macro. The learner edits the actual-argument text and the variable values (a, cnt). Before anything is revealed they choose 'what the compiler sees' from 3-4 candidate expansions, then the resulting value and how many times bump() ran. A scrubber then steps through: (1) argument binding, with default chips filling empty slots; (2) substitution, with each pasted fragment marked by where it came from (argument text with a dashed underline, body text plain); (3) `" and `` processing and inner-macro expansion; (4) a parse tree that shows the precedence regrouping, with a bump() call counter that ticks only in the evaluated branch. Each error preset names the rule it breaks and its clause. Needs a new pure model, src/lib/sv-macro-model.ts (expandMacro per §22.5.1 plus a tiny integer evaluator with a side-effecting bump()).

needs.concept: The disable protocol (§35.9). An import enters the disabled state only when an export it called returns. The export returns 1 (a). The import task must return 1 (b). An imported function must call svAckDisabledState (c). No further export calls are allowed (d), and breaking (b) to (d) is a fatal error. Output values after a disable are undefined. A disable aimed at the export itself does not put the import in the disabled state.

(6) Broken C: ignores the 1 and calls sv_send_word again, so the model reports a fatal protocol error (d), worded generically because the message is tool-specific. needs.concept: Call-chain context (§35.5.3, H.9.3). The context property is not promoted down the chain, so an export call from a non-context import in the chain is an error. svPutUserData/svGetUserData give one C object per instance per key.

needs.where: 'The layered testbench you can already build' (L35-88, first ArchitectureDiagram) and Make It Work > 'How to read and extend it', steps 1-2 'Trace one write' / 'Trace one read' (L862-864)
needs.concept: How one transaction moves through the layered bench, and the cycle timing that makes the bench race-free. drv_cb drives land in Re-NBA and reach the DUT flops at the next edge (IEEE 1800-2023 §14.16). mon_cb samples pre-edge values, because the default input skew is 1step (§14.3, §14.13). The read is registered, which is why the monitor needs rd_pending. gen2drv is bounded to 1, so the generator runs one item ahead. The scoreboard's reference queue pushes on accepted writes and pops on accepted reads.
needs.interaction: New component, e.g. LayeredFifoBenchTrace, mode="trace", with a pure model src/lib/layered-fifo-bench-model.ts. The model simulates sync_fifo, fifo_drv, fifo_mon, fifo_sb and fifo_cov exactly as the listing is written, with a seeded LCG. The learner scrubs edge by edge (Left/Right, Home) through a short preset of about 12 items. The preset includes a read that completes on the same edge as a new write, a write when full, a read when empty, and the drain reads. The learner picks one transaction to follow. A token moves gen -> gen2drv -> drv -> bus -> dut -> mon -> mon2sb/mon2cov -> sb/cov on the lesson's BlockDiagram. Beside it, a CycleWaveform (clk, rst_n, wr_en, wr_data, rd_en, rd_data, full, empty) marks drive and sample points. Before a read is published, the learner predicts the edge it will appear on and the rd_data it will carry. Answer: one edge after rd_en was sampled, with the value the flop loaded at the accepting edge. Side panels show the mailbox contents as handles (arrows to objects), the scoreboard model queue with EXP/ACT and pass/fail glyphs, the coverage bins that light up, and the log lines the listing would print. Presets: 'trace one write', 'trace one read', 'write when full', 'read when empty'. Fidelity: deterministic educational model. State the one process order the model assumes wherever §4.7 leaves the order open.

needs.where: Make It Work > 'Debug challenge: three mutants' (L869-895, about 545 words of reveal-only prose)
needs.concept: The log signatures of three classic layered-bench bugs. Mutant 1 reuses the monitor's handle. Mutant 2 ignores the one-cycle read latency. Mutant 3 ends the test when the generator returns, which can give a false pass.
needs.interaction: The same new component in mode="debug", with initialMutant 1, 2 or 3. The learner applies a mutant; the changed line is shown in a code panel generated from model data. They predict the symptom by picking one of four log excerpts, for example: 'mismatches start where a READ completes with a new WRITE, pending != 0'; 'every read shows the previous read's data'; 'mismatches=0 but matches < total and FAIL=0'. Then they run it. For mutant 1 the view highlights the first divergent edge and the two mailbox entries pointing at one object. For mutant 2 the waveform cursor sits where mon_cb samples the stale rd_data. For mutant 3 it shows the final SCB_SUMMARY and the PASS line. The learner then picks a fix, graded by the model, with a three-hint HintLadder. Accuracy, mutant 1: its symptom requires the monitor to run both publish calls before the scoreboard resumes. Simulators usually do this, but IEEE 1800-2023 §4.7 lets a simulator suspend between statements, so the visual must state this as an assumption. Accuracy, mutant 3: what happens at the last edge depends on the process order between the env thread and the monitor and scoreboard waking on the same mon_cb event. The model should explore both orders (as exploreOrderings does) and show both outcomes. That is exactly the lesson's 'the two extra clocks are not always enough'.

needs.concept: No mechanism is free; each brings one silent failure. A late override does nothing. get returns 0 and the vif stays null. A plain $error is not counted by get_severity_count.

needs.where: ### Verbosity: which information messages print (lines 85-100), right after the traced table at line 94
needs.concept: The verbosity threshold: a `uvm_info prints only if its verbosity is <= the effective maximum. The effective maximum follows a precedence: a verbosity set for (severity,ID) wins over one set for an ID, which wins over the component's maximum (§6.4.3.1). Warnings, errors and fatals always pass. A filtered message is neither printed nor counted. Spine misconception 1.
needs.interaction: A vertical verbosity ruler for each of two components (uvm_test_top, chk): NONE 0, LOW 100, MEDIUM 200, HIGH 300, FULL 400, plus DEBUG 500 marked uvm-core only. Each message is a chip on the rung of its verbosity. The learner drags the component threshold, or adds one per-ID override (+uvm_set_verbosity=uvm_test_top.chk,CHK,UVM_HIGH,build). Before reveal, they tick which chips will print and predict the UVM_INFO count. The reveal lights the chips at or below the line and greys the rest with a 'not created, not counted' tag. The CFG warning, MISMATCH error and NO_VIF fatal sit on the UVM_NONE rung and print at every setting.

needs.where: ### Ending a run: normally, by timeout, or by quit count (lines 328-365), before the 'Two ways a run ends' SequenceDiagram at line 341 (closes the text-heavy stretch 317-340); answers Quiz Q4 and Q10 and the Break-it '+UVM_MAX_QUIT_COUNT=1' row
needs.concept: Normal end vs die(). On a normal end every phase runs, then report_summarize and $finish. die(), triggered by any report with UVM_EXIT (a fatal, PH_TIMEOUT, or the error that reaches the quit count), calls pre_abort bottom-up, then report_summarize, then $finish (F.7.3.2 a-f). No later phase runs, so the check_phase guard, CHK_DONE and VERDICT lines are missing. An SV $fatal ends the run with no UVM summary at all.

They predict which of five lines will appear (NO_CHECKS guard, CHK_DONE, VERDICT, Quit count reached!, the summary block). Then they step a phase strip (build, connect, end_of_elaboration, start_of_simulation, run, extract, check, report, final, report_summarize, $finish). On die() the strip jumps to pre_abort, report_summarize, $finish and greys out the phases that never run.

needs.concept: Variable vs net on a passive agent's interface. A variable that is a clocking-block output may not also be continuously driven (§14.16.2), and a DUT output port implies such a driver (§23.3.3.2). needs.concept: get() sees only entries whose T is a matching type (IEEE 1800-2023 §6.22.1, §8.25). A typedef rename matches. int unsigned and bit signed [31:0] match bit [31:0] and int respectively (rule e plus §6.11.1). int vs bit [31:0] (sign) and logic vs bit (4-state) do not match, and uvm_bitstream_t matches neither. Modport and interface parameter values are part of a vif type (§25.9). Class types match only themselves, and the same class declared in two packages is two types. Assigning a no-modport vif to a modport vif is legal (§25.9). This is assessment misconception 1.
