needs.concept: lock() and grab() are both exclusive until released. They differ in where the request enters the arbitration queue: a lock at the back, a grab at the front (§14.2.5.5, §14.2.5.6). So a waiting grab is served before a waiting lock. Spine misconception 3.

The learner predicts who gets the sequencer at unlock and sees the grant, plus bg_seq waiting until ungrab(). A second step shows a holder that ends without unlock(): SEQFINERR in uvm-core and silent starvation until then. Only use cases where IEEE 1800.2-2020 and uvm-core agree, or label uvm-core-only behaviour.

needs.where: 'Expert: where the two decisions meet', first two bullets (lines 580-581)
needs.concept: If a virtual sequence forks two children onto the same sequencer, from then on the sequencer's arbitration interleaves their items. needs.where: Sequence library paragraph (line 219) and tool-table row (213)
needs.concept: A uvm_sequence_library is itself a sequence that picks registered members and runs them one after another on its sequencer. UVM_SEQ_LIB_RAND randomizes select_rand, RANDC randomizes select_randc (random-cyclic), ITEM emits only REQ items with no sequences, and USER calls select_sequence() (§14.4, Annex F.2.4.3). It cannot express cross-agent order.

needs.where: 'Expert: ending a test that has background stimulus' (lines 601-608)
needs.concept: How background stimulus ends: at task-phase end, uvm-core kills the running threads, and §9.7 kills their descendants too. They predict when run_phase ends and which items complete, then see the objection-count line, the body() return, the phase-end line, the killed threads and any warning (SEQPRTZMB, PH_TIMEOUT).

needs.where: ### The four driver calls compared (lines 66-110) and ## Push Further / ### Expert: the call matrix inside uvm-core 2020.3.1 (lines 444-453)
needs.concept: What each fetch call does: get_next_item, try_next_item, peek and get. When the sequence's finish_item() returns (at item_done vs at fetch for get()), whether the item stays in the one-slot request FIFO, and what a second fetch before item_done() does. The two uvm-core flags explain the matrix: sequence_item_requested and get_next_item_called. get_next_item sets both. peek sets only sequence_item_requested. get() is m_safe_select_item(0) followed by item_done(). try_next_item returns early with its own error when get_next_item_called is set.
needs.interaction: A fetch-call explorer. The learner picks the driver's first call (get_next_item / try_next_item / peek / get) and an optional second action before item_done (same call again, get(), get_next_item, try_next_item, item_done after get, nothing). They predict two things: when burst_seq's finish_item() returns relative to the 10 ns of driving, and what the second call returns and logs. Then they step through seq/sqr/drv lanes, with the request-FIFO slot chip and the two flag chips lighting as each uvm-core line runs, and the log shows exactly one of: 'Get_next_item called twice…', 'get_next_item/try_next_item called twice…', SQRBADITMDN, or nothing (peek twice, peek then get_next_item, get_next_item then get). An 'Expert' toggle reveals the flag chips, so the call matrix in Push Further can be read straight off the visual.

needs.concept: Polling-driver timing inside one time slot. try_next_item waits m_wait_for_sequences_count wait_for_sequences() calls (one NBA region by default) before choosing and again after granting. needs.where: ### How a response finds its sequence (lines 112-153), including the 'Response routing in uvm-core 2020.3.1' SequenceDiagram and Rules and pitfalls
needs.concept: Routing by ids: set_id_info copies sequence_id and transaction_id. The four driver paths (item_done(rsp), put_response, put, rsp_port.write) all end in uvm_sequencer_param_base::put_response, which checks in this order: null response is SQRPUT 'Driver put a null response'; sequence_id -1 is SQRPUT 'null sequence_id'; sequence not found is a UVM_WARNING and the response is dropped; use_response_handler set calls response_handler() at once; otherwise the sequence's put_response casts to RSP (PUTRSP) and pushes onto the queue unless it is full. Sending the same response twice queues a stale copy.
needs.interaction: A response-routing switchboard. Toggles: rsp built new + set_id_info / new without set_id_info / req.clone() without set_id_info / null; driver path (the four, with rsp_port connected or not); 'also call put_response after item_done(rsp)'; response type matches the sequence's RSP or not; sequence still in body() or already returned; use_response_handler on/off; queue full or not. The learner predicts the outcome from a fixed list (response_handler called, queued, queued twice, UVM_FATAL SQRPUT, UVM_FATAL PUTRSP, UVM_WARNING 'Dropping response for sequence N', silently dropped on overflow, never delivered). Then a response token moves down the check funnel and stops at the deciding check, labelled with the uvm-core function and the IEEE clause. A follow-up get_response() chip shows what the next call returns (e.g. the stale duplicate).
needs.existing: AnimatedUvmSequenceDriverHandshakeDiagram preset rsp_no_id covers one branch (SQRPUT)
needs.gap: Needs a pure routeResponse(spec) in src/lib/uvm-sequencer-model.ts that mirrors uvm_sequencer_param_base::put_response, uvm_sequence::put_response (PUTRSP) and uvm_sequence_base::put_base_response (depth and error-report bit). The rsp_port.write path goes through analysis_write(), which has its own cast fatal ANALWRT 'Failure to cast analysis port write item' (uvm_sequencer_param_base.svh). The lesson does not mention it yet, so the visual must not show PUTRSP for that path. Small new component (e.g. ResponseRoutingExplorer) reusing UvmLog from the handshake diagram.

needs.where: ### The response queue and how it overflows (lines 155-163) and ### Kata: collect by transaction_id, and watch the queue overflow (lines 649-701)
needs.concept: Each sequence's response queue holds 8 entries by default. IEEE 1800.2-2020 §14.2.7.4/§14.2.7.5 say overflow is an error by default; uvm-core 2020.3.1 drops silently because response_queue_error_report_enabled has no initializer. get_response(rsp, tid) waits for one id and leaves the rest, so a pipelined 'send all, then collect by id' sequence waits forever on a dropped tid.
needs.interaction: A queue strip of 8 slots with an overflow bin beside it, driven by a time scrubber through the kata. The driver answers pairs newest-first every 10 ns, and the sequence collects only after its 12th finish_item at 50 ns. Controls: depth (8 / 12 / -1), set_response_queue_error_report_enabled(0/1), collection strategy (after all sends / forked collector while sending / response handler). Before stepping, the learner predicts which get_response(rsp, tid) blocks forever and what the log shows. On reveal, tids 10 and 9 drop into the bin at 50 ns with no log line (or two 'Response queue overflow, response was dropped' errors when reporting is on), tids 1-8 are collected by id, and get_response(rsp, 9) stays highlighted while 12 and 11 arrive at 60 ns. A side note shows the IEEE vs uvm-core difference.

needs.gap: rsp_overflow has no get() pipelined driver, no transaction_id-keyed get_response, and no depth or error-report controls in the UI. needs.where: ### Pipelined drivers and out-of-order responses (lines 165-204) and ## Make It Work: the out-of-order read bench, Expected output and Break it on purpose (lines 243-421)
needs.concept: With get(), finish_item is released when the driver takes the item, so several requests are outstanding at once. The driver keeps them and answers out of order with put(rsp). The response handler matches responses by transaction_id. It is a function running in the driver's thread, and with an item_done(rsp) driver it runs before finish_item returns. body() must wait for the last response. A reused item keeps transaction_id 1 because send_request() assigns an id only while it is -1.
needs.interaction: The Make It Work bench as a stepped run: seq/sqr/drv lanes, plus the driver's 'pending' queue chips and the sequence's expected[tid] map. Presets: the bench as written, then each Break-it mutation: (1) no use_response_handler, (2) handler plus repeat get_response, (3) create() moved above the repeat, (4) no set_id_info, (5) no final wait, with and without a 50 ns drain time. One more preset uses an item_done(rsp) driver where expected[] is recorded after finish_item. Before each run the learner commits a prediction of the end state and the first telling log line: PH_TIMEOUT with nothing else; RSPID 'unexpected response tid=1' at 10 and 20 ns; SQRPUT at 10 ns; only two RSP lines and a clean report; Dropping response warnings at 20 ns. A 'driver reorder' control (in order / newest first) shows that matching by tid makes order irrelevant. The generated log for the clean preset must reproduce the Expected output: took 1,2 at 0; RSP 2,1 at 10; took 3,4 at 10; RSP 4,3 at 20.
needs.existing: AnimatedUvmSequenceDriverHandshakeDiagram (get_next_item, in-order, one response per item only)
needs.gap: Needs model support for: get() fetch, a driver-held pending list with a reorder policy and latency, put(rsp), transaction_id assignment only when the id is -1, use_response_handler with handler-before-finish_item timing for item_done(rsp), a sequence end that unregisters its id (Dropping warning), and phase end with drain time stopping the driver. Best done as a new scenario family in uvm-sequencer-model.ts (e.g. pipelinedScenario(id)) with a component such as PipelinedResponseExplorer that reuses the exported QueueChips and UvmLog.

needs.where: ### Hang signatures and triage (lines 206-231) and ### Debug challenge: the five hang scenarios (lines 645-647)
needs.concept: The four-step triage: find the blocked side (start_item / finish_item / get_response vs driver fetch / driver pin-level code), match the log signature (or notice there is none), probe the sequencer, then fix and rerun with a short timeout. Silent hangs (missing response, dropped tid, lock, driver stuck in its own code) are found only by locating the blocked side.
needs.interaction: A triage mode in the handshake explorer. The lanes are hidden. The learner sees only the log at the timeout and may press probes (sqr.get_current_item(), last_req(), last_rsp(), convert2string()); each probe reveals its value at the hang and uses a HintLadder rung. They must name the blocked side and call, then choose cause and fix from options. Then the lanes reveal and the run replays. Cases drawn from the triage table: missing item_done, double get, SQRPUT, PUTRSP, sequence waiting in get_response, dropped tid, Dropping response (sequence not found), driver stuck in pin code (get_current_item returns A3, no 'called twice' error), no driver asking, SQRBADITMDN after get(). The page's Debug challenge would point here instead of back to the scenario menu with the debrief removed.

needs.concept: stop_sequences() kills every sequence and, in uvm-core, empties the request FIFO with UVM_INFO 'Sequences stopped.  Removing request from sequencer fifo'. A late response for a killed or finished sequence is dropped with the 'sequence not found' warning. kill() in uvm-core skips post_body/post_start.

needs.where: ### The six arbitration modes (lines 89-132), plus the Assessment focus misconception 'SEQ_ARB_WEIGHTED is strict priority'
needs.concept: Each built-in mode is the answer to two questions: is priority ignored, used as a weight or used as a rank, and are ties broken by age or at random? WEIGHTED is odds, not order.
needs.interaction: One frozen queue (for example A 100 oldest, B 300, C 100, no lock). The learner commits a prediction per mode: a definite winner for FIFO and STRICT_FIFO, odds for WEIGHTED, RANDOM and STRICT_RANDOM. The reveal then shows one row per mode: the deterministic winner, or an exact probability bar (B 300/500 = 60 % under WEIGHTED, 1/3 each under RANDOM, B 100 % under STRICT_RANDOM because it is the only top-priority request) beside a seeded 200-grant histogram from the model. The learner then edits priorities or queue order and watches the rows change. The rules are the ones in uvm-core m_choose_next_request(): WEIGHTED uses $urandom_range(sum-1,0) walked cumulatively, and STRICT_* first keep only the highest priority.
needs.existing: SequencerArbitrationSandbox (fifo, strict_fifo and weighted presets, mode switch, SeedCheck histogram)
needs.gap: No compare-across-modes view: the sandbox shows one mode at a time, and exact odds appear only for the first contested decision of a random mode. Add a 'Compare modes' tab to the sandbox, like TemporalLogicExplorer's compare-the-family view, computed from uvm-sequencer-model (sampleDecisionWinners plus exact odds). UVM_SEQ_ARB_USER is not modelled, so label that row 'your rule'.

needs.where: ### lock() and grab() Experiment: 'Scroll back to the arbitration sandbox' (lines 193-199), and Push Further grabs among grabs / nested locks (lines 599-602)
needs.concept: lock() pushes its request to the back of the queue and grab() pushes it to the front. A granted request moves into lock_list and blocks every request that is not from the holder or one of its descendants. Neither one pre-empts a current holder. A forgotten unlock() lasts until start() ends (SEQFINERR). A later grab is queued ahead of an earlier waiting grab. lock(); lock(); unlock() still leaves one entry blocking.
needs.interaction: A second sandbox embed sits right next to the lock/grab text, opened on the lock() preset. The learner predicts grant #2, then reads the queue chips and lock_list per decision. They switch to Forgot unlock() and predict when C runs (70 ns, SEQFINERR), then grab vs lock (C before B). Two new presets follow. 'Two grabs': A holds a lock, B grabs at 2 ns, C grabs at 4 ns, predict who runs after A (C, because of push_front). 'Nested lock': B locks twice and unlocks once, predict whether C runs before B's start() ends.
needs.existing: SequencerArbitrationSandbox (lock, forgot_unlock and grab_vs_lock presets; DecisionList with QueueChips and lock_list)
needs.gap: No initialPreset prop, so the lesson has to send learners back up the page. Add initialPreset: ArbitrationPresetId. The model already uses push_front for a grab, but arbitrationScenario has no 'two grabs' or 'nested lock' preset. The editor form (one 'Before items' take) cannot represent two lock ops, so formFromSpec would lose a nested lock: it needs a lock-count control or a read-only mode for curated presets. Also add a unit test showing that a holder's second lock is granted at once and that unlock removes one lock_list entry (uvm-core m_unlock_req uses find_first_index).

needs.where: ### Waiting for a resource: is_relevant() and wait_for_relevant() (lines 262-340), ### Throttling without stalling the driver (lines 342-387), and the Kata 'credits without stalling' (lines 813-859)
needs.concept: Where a sequence waits decides whether the driver stalls. Waiting before start_item() queues no request. is_relevant() keeps the request queued but skipped at each choice, and wait_for_relevant() is called only when nothing can be granted. Waiting after start_item() or in pre_do() happens after the grant, so the driver idles while other traffic is ready.
needs.interaction: Three lanes on one shared timeline run the kata scenario: FIFO, bulk n=2 or 4, credit_seq n=2, credits=1, +1 credit at 35 ns. The lanes are (1) wait before start_item, (2) is_relevant + wait_for_relevant, (3) wait after start_item (or in pre_do). The learner predicts each lane's grant times and end time. The reveal draws driver-idle spans hatched and marks the sequencer's is_relevant() and wait_for_relevant() calls. The oracle is the lesson's own trace: n=2 grants at 0 bulk, 10 cs, 20 bulk, 30 none, 35 cs, ending at 45 ns; n=4 ends at 60 ns for lanes 1 and 2 and at 65 ns for lane 3. Debug toggles: 'is_relevant overridden alone' leads to UVM_FATAL [RELMSM]. 'wait_for_relevant returns at once' leads to [SEQRELEVANTLOOP] after the default 10 zero-time passes (uvm-core m_wait_for_available_sequence).
needs.gap: None of the catalog covers it. The uvm-sequencer-model header says is_relevant() is always 1. Extend the model with a credit pool (credit events over time), an is_relevant gate per sequence, wait_for_relevant (including the RELMSM and zero-time-loop cases) and an item op that holds after the grant (pre_do or wait-after-start_item). Then add a compare-two-executions view, either as a 'Credits' tab in SequencerArbitrationSandbox or as a new src/components/visuals/ThrottleCompareVisualizer.tsx on the same model. Pin the kata tables in tests/lib/uvm-sequencer-model.test.ts.

needs.where: ### When the sequencer arbitrates (lines 52-87) and the Quick Take's four deciders (line 16)
needs.concept: One decision is a funnel. The driver asks, uvm-core waits one NBA region, then the sequencer considers queued item requests only, drops those blocked by lock_list, drops those whose is_relevant() is 0, and lets the mode's rule pick among the rest. A request made after the choice waits for the next one.
needs.interaction: Scrub across the grant decisions of any sandbox run. For the selected decision, the learner first predicts which requests survive each stage. Then the queue chips animate one stage at a time: struck as blocked, struck as not relevant, rule applied, granted. A 'late request' toggle adds a request after the choice and shows it waiting for the next decision.

needs.gap: DecisionList is a static list with no stage-by-stage stepper or PlaybackControls scrubber. The not-relevant stage cannot be shown until the model has is_relevant (see the throttling need).

needs.where: ### Priority (lines 134-156), 'The classic mistake', and quiz Q3
needs.concept: Where a request's priority comes from and when it freezes. start(sqr, parent, p) with p = -1 gives a root 100 and a child its parent's priority. set_priority() before start() is overwritten. start_item(item, sp) captures sp, or get_priority() when sp < 0, into the request. Only WEIGHTED and STRICT_* read it. A priority of 0 or less read by them gives SEQITEMPRI.
needs.interaction: A priority-provenance tracer. The learner picks one way of setting priority: start(sqr,null,300); set_priority(300) then start(sqr); set_priority(300) inside body before start_item; start_item(req,500); a child started with the default under a parent at 300; or start(sqr,null,0) under WEIGHTED. They predict the priority the queued request carries and whether it changes the grant. The reveal steps start() to m_priority to start_item to the request's priority, with the overwrite or the fatal highlighted, and then runs the grant in the sandbox.
needs.existing: SequencerArbitrationSandbox (start() priority per sequence, 50-500)
needs.gap: The model's SeqOp item already has an optional priority (start_item(req, p)), but the UI does not expose it. set_priority-before-start overwrite, parent inheritance and the priority-0 SEQPRI/SEQITEMPRI paths are not modelled. Add these to uvm-sequencer-model (checked against uvm_sequence_base start() lines 320-339 and m_get_seq_item_priority) and a priority-source control to the sandbox.

needs.where: ### lock() and grab(): 'Who is not blocked by a lock' and the child experiment (lines 185-191)
needs.concept: The lock holder and its descendants (is_child walks the parent chain) are exempt. A child started without the parent argument is a new root, so its own parent's lock blocks it, and the result is a silent deadlock.
needs.interaction: Already embedded. The learner ticks 'top_seq calls lock() first', sets read_seq to start(m_sequencer), predicts what happens at its first start_item(), sees the deadlock trace, then switches to start(m_sequencer, this).

needs.gap: No props, so the lesson must tell the learner which boxes to tick. Add initialRootLocks and initialReadStyle (or a preset="lock-deadlock") so the embed opens on the case this section teaches.

needs.where: 'Locks from a virtual sequence' and the two release rules (lines 234-260), quiz Q9
needs.concept: lock, grab, unlock and ungrab default to the sequence's own sequencer. A virtual sequence must name the physical sequencer in both the grab and the release. A bare ungrab() acts on the virtual sequencer: UVM_WARNING [SQRUNL], and data_sqr stays grabbed. When the virtual sequence was started with start(null), a bare ungrab() is UVM_FATAL [UNLOCK] and a bare grab() is UVM_FATAL [GRAB].

needs.concept: avail_sequences holds queue indexes of the unblocked, relevant item requests, already filtered. The override must return one of them or the run stops with a fatal. needs.where: Push Further: 'Expert: locks, killed processes and cleanup' (lines 652-658)
needs.concept: A lock belongs to the sequence object. What happens depends on which process dies: an inner thread of body (lock kept until start() ends, SEQFINERR), the start() caller (SEQPRTZMB then kill()), body's own process (SEQBDYZMB), or a lock request whose caller died (SEQLCKZMB). kill() and stop_sequences() remove requests and locks, and in uvm-core post_body and post_start do not run.
needs.interaction: The learner picks what is killed, predicts the message, when the lock is released, and whether post_body runs. The reveal shows the outcome.

staticVisuals: After the Quick Take (before line 20): a one-glance 'one grant, four inputs' ArchitectureDiagram. Three sequence nodes feed a sequencer node holding 'arbitration queue', 'lock_list' and 'mode'. A driver node pulls with an edge labelled 'get_next_item(): asks'. Labels name priority, lock()/grab() and is_relevant() where they act. Next to it, a two-column table 'Analogy says / The real sequencer does' for the three places the air-traffic analogy breaks (line 18).

After the six-mode table (line 102): a 3x2 mode-matrix figure. Rows: priority ignored / weight / rank. Columns: ties by age / at random. Cells: FIFO, RANDOM, (weight-by-age empty), WEIGHTED, STRICT_FIFO, STRICT_RANDOM. USER sits outside as 'your rule'. This makes the lesson's 'read the table as two questions' a picture.

In the WEIGHTED worked example (line 104): a number-line figure. A covers [0,100), B covers [100,400), with the draw temp = $urandom_range(399,0) and the cumulative walk from uvm-core m_choose_next_request(). Caption: 75 % / 25 %, odds not order, A never locked out.

In ### Priority (after line 142): a priority-flow diagram. start(sqr, parent, p) leads, for p = -1, to root 100 or the parent's priority, stored in m_priority. set_priority() rewrites m_priority, but before start() it is overwritten. start_item(item, sp): if sp < 0, get_priority() is used, and the value is captured in the request. Readers: WEIGHTED and STRICT_* read it; FIFO and RANDOM ignore it; a value of 0 or less gives SEQITEMPRI.

In ### lock() and grab() (after the table at line 183): a three-frame step reveal of the arbitration queue and lock_list. Frame 1: A holds the lock. Frame 2: B lock() is pushed to the back and C grab() to the front. Frame 3: A unlocks, C is granted, then C ungrabs and B is granted. It uses the existing VisualRecap SVG's chip vocabulary (dashed = lock request).

At 'Who is not blocked by a lock' (line 185): a small ArchitectureDiagram of the sequence tree. top_seq holds the lock. read_seq started with start(sqr, this) is a child and is exempt (ok state). read_seq started with start(sqr) is a separate root, blocked (error state), with a causal edge 'top_seq waits in read_seq.start()' that closes the deadlock loop.

After the virtual-sequence SequenceDiagram (line 260): an outcome table for grab argument x release argument x how irq_vseq was started. Outcomes: clean; SQRUNL with data_sqr still grabbed; UVM_FATAL [UNLOCK]; UVM_FATAL [GRAB].

Columns: request queued?, granted?, driver stalls?, checked at grant time?, use when. Plus a TimingDiagram of the kata's driver lane (grants at 0, 10, 20, idle 30-35 ns, 35) with a marker at 35 ns 'credit arrives'.

In ### Debugging starvation and deadlock (before the symptom table, line 393): a symptom-to-probe triage flowchart (ArchitectureDiagram with causal edges). 'Driver idle, no errors' leads to is_grabbed()/current_grabber(). 'One stream never runs' leads to get_arbitration() and priorities. 'Hang right after lock()' leads to child.is_blocked(). Message IDs lead to the matching table row.

In the same section (line 404): an annotated convert2string decode figure, '-- arb i/id/type: 0/2/SEQ_TYPE_REQ 1/3/SEQ_TYPE_LOCK' and '-- lock_list i/id: 0/1', with labels i = queue index, id = sequence id on this sequencer, type = request kind. The format matches uvm-core convert2string().

needs.where: Registering members (L63-118), next to the static ArchitectureDiagram at L95
needs.concept: Two queues, not one. The macros (static bit initializer -> LIBTYPE::m_add_typewide_sequence) fill the subtype's static m_typewide_sequences. The subtype's non-virtual init_sequence_library() copies that list into this object's protected sequences queue. start() reads only that queue. add_typewide_sequence() after construction does not change existing objects, and add_sequence() edits one instance.
needs.interaction: Register tab of a new SequenceLibraryLab. The learner toggles 'constructor calls init_sequence_library()' and, for each member (wr_seq, rd_seq, err_seq), picks how it registers: macro naming mem_seq_lib, macro naming another library, add_typewide_sequence() before create, add_typewide_sequence() after create, lib.add_sequence() on this instance, or not compiled. A second instance lib2 is created as well. The learner predicts how many members lib and lib2 hold and what lib.start() logs, then sees the static list and both object queues fill (the arrows from the static diagram, now live) and the outcome: SEQLIB/NOSEQS or SEQLIB/START with N members. A 'register twice' switch with IEEE 1800.2-2020 / uvm-core 2020.3.1 columns shows four cases: the standard ignores the repeat (§14.4.5.1-§14.4.5.4); a second macro in one class does not compile; add_sequence() drops the duplicate (m_dyn_check); a repeated add_typewide_sequence() on a subtype is kept, because the macro's add_typewide_sequence() calls the base m_static_check(), which scans the base class's list. All of this comes from a pure model in src/lib/uvm-sequence-library-model.ts, which mirrors uvm_sequence_library.svh and the uvm_sequence_library_utils / uvm_add_to_seq_lib macros.

needs.where: Selection modes and counts (L120-155): the 'Predict first' table at L141-149 and 'The count only changes when the library is randomized' at L139
needs.concept: What one start() runs in each selection mode for a given member list and count: RAND (uniform index, repeats, skips), RANDC (each N consecutive picks are one permutation; a fresh cycle each start()), ITEM (REQ items, no members), USER (default select_sequence() is round robin by index, 0..max, then wraps). Plus the rule that sequence_count stays 10 unless the library is randomized.
needs.interaction: Run tab of SequenceLibraryLab. Controls: members (3 by default, editable), selection_mode, min/max_random_count, a 'call lib.randomize()' toggle, a 'set_sequencer() before randomize()' toggle, seed, verbosity (LOW/HIGH/FULL). Predict-then-reveal gates: (1) how many iterations SEQLIB/START reports; (2) for USER with no override, which index list runs; (3) for RANDC with count 6, the per-type counts. The reveal is a pick strip (one tile per pick, named <type>:<n> from sequences_executed+1, with RANDC cycle boundaries drawn), a SEQLIB/DSTRB bar per type, and the generated log, filtered by verbosity (START/END at LOW, DSTRB at HIGH, EXEC and SPRINT at FULL). A scrubber steps the picks. The model has to reproduce uvm-core body(): the null-sequencer fatal; NOSEQS checked before the mode case, so an ITEM-mode library with no members also errors and sends nothing; RANDC draws every index into a queue and then executes; USER returns >= size give USER_FAIL and execute a REQ item; and the counter, sequences_executed and seqs_distrib are not reset between two start() calls on the same object. Accuracy note for the content owner: the quiz feedback at L750, 'Members are irrelevant in ITEM mode', does not hold in uvm-core 2020.3.1, because an empty library reports SEQLIB/NOSEQS even in ITEM mode. A preset 'make-it-work' (RANDC, 3 members, 6 picks, 10 ns per item) shows the L520-545 log on a 0-60 ns timeline.

needs.where: 'What the table shows' (L151-155) and the interview item 'the member that never runs' (L629-638)
needs.concept: A short RAND run can skip a member: with N members and k picks, the chance that a given member never runs is ((N-1)/N)^k, for example (7/8)^10, about 26%. RANDC guarantees every member once per full cycle of N picks. So a member that never runs in 1000 seeds is a registration bug, not bad luck.
needs.interaction: Seeds tab of SequenceLibraryLab. Sliders for members N and picks per run k, and a RAND/RANDC toggle. The learner predicts the percentage of seeds in which err_seq never runs, then the lab samples 1000 seeded runs from the same model (seeded RNG, no Math.random) and shows a histogram of err_seq's count per run next to the exact ((N-1)/N)^k figure, labelled as exact vs sampled. For RANDC with k >= N the zero bar is empty, and when k is a multiple of N every bar sits at k/N. A final prompt: '1000 seeds, zero runs: what do you check first?', with options taken from the interview question.

needs.where: ### Expert: One-to-many and many-to-one translation (line 698) and ### Kata: a fragmenting translation sequence (line 863)
needs.concept: Fragmentation. One packet's to_bytes() stream (id, length, data) is cut into frames of at most N payload bytes, with more=1 on every frame except the last. ip_sqr.item_done() is called once, after the last fragment. ip_mon's pending buffer grows until a more=0 frame arrives. Aggregation breaks the 'delivered' meaning.
needs.interaction: Byte-strip lab. The learner sets packet length (1-16) and max payload per frame (unlimited | 4 | 2) and predicts the number of frames, their more bits, and the time 'packet 0 delivered' prints. The reveal shows the strip split into frames on the driver lane at 10 ns each, ip_mon's pending buffer filling and then rebuilding a new ip_packet, and the single ip_sqr.item_done(). Mutation toggles from the kata: item_done inside the while loop gives UVM_FATAL SQRBADITMDN on the second fragment, because the request FIFO is empty (uvm-core item_done). more=0 on every frame makes ip_mon report 'malformed packet' on the first frame, since size 4 is not len+2. Payload bytes are seeded, so later frames show their real, data-dependent outcome. Default preset is len=5, max 4: frames of 4 and 3 bytes at 10 and 20 ns, delivered at 20 ns. Aggregation tab: two packets per frame, where the upper finish_item returns before the frame is sent.

needs.concept: What the parent argument changes. With `this`, the parent's pre_do/mid_do/post_do run, the child inherits the parent's priority, and lock() exempts the child (is_blocked/is_child). Without it the child is a root sequence: the parent's hooks do not run, priority defaults to 100, and the parent's own lock blocks it, so the parent deadlocks inside start().

needs.where: ### Where the translation sequence lives, and how it ends (line 275) and ### Expert: Ending the test with an endless layer (line 713)
needs.concept: A forever translation sequence does not keep the test alive; only objections do. Once the last objection drops, phase_ready_to_end (§13.1.4.3.2) lets the layering env call xlate.kill() (§14.2.5.11). Without that call, uvm-core 2020.3.1's process guard reports SEQPRTZMB when the run phase kills the starting process. That is uvm-core implementation behaviour, not IEEE 1800.2-2020.

needs.where: ### Expert: Reset and restart of a layered stack (line 707)
needs.concept: Killing xlate between ip_sqr.get_next_item() and item_done() leaves the get_next_item_called flag set and the packet at the head of ip_sqr's request FIFO. The restarted xlate logs 'Get_next_item called twice without item_done or get in between' and gets the old packet again, because m_safe_select_item peeks it. stop_sequences() on both sequencers (§15.3.2.14) kills the registered sequences, clears the flags and flushes the FIFO.
needs.interaction: Reset preset. The learner chooses the recovery (kill xlate only | stop_sequences on ip_sqr only | on eth_agt.sqr only | on both) and predicts the first log line after restart and which packet is sent next. The reveal shows ip_sqr's flag and FIFO before and after, and which sequences survive on each sequencer.

This depends on recording being enabled on sqr/drv/mon, on whether the driver records items itself, on when disable_auto_item_recording() is called, and on parent_handle. The behaviour follows uvm-core: start() calls begin_tr(seq) on a stream named after the root sequence, start_item calls begin_tr(item, root-seq stream, label "Transactions") after the grant, finish_item calls end_tr after item_done only if auto recording is still on, and m_begin_tr looks up parent_seq.m_tr_recorder. 2D because viewers draw streams as rows over time; 3D would add nothing.

needs.where: ### Queue order: APPEND, PREPEND and type-wide copies (lines 244-268, trace table at 255-260)
needs.concept: Order is queue order. The first instance add copies the type-wide queue as it is at that moment. UVM_PREPEND goes in front of earlier entries, including earlier prepends. A later type-wide add goes into the type-wide queue and into every instance queue that already exists (§10.7.2.3.1; uvm-core m_add_tw_cbs). The result is visible in which CRC log_cb prints, 0x5A or 0xA5.
needs.interaction: A 'queue builder' step-through with a scrubber over a list of add/delete/callback_mode calls. Before each step the learner predicts the type-wide, agt0.drv and agt1.drv queues, by ordering chips or picking from options. Then the step is revealed, with the queue each driver walks (instance or type-wide) and the CRC that log_cb prints on agt0's first packet. Presets: 'lesson-table' (the four rows of the table at 255-260), 'late-type-wide' (log_cb added after err_cb, so it logs the corrupted CRC), 'double-prepend', 'mode-vs-delete' (one object in two queues), and an expert 'empty-queue re-seed'.

Add a mode="queue" with an initialPreset prop driven by the existing primitives. Two model issues first. (1) cbAdd seeds an instance queue only when none exists, but uvm-core 2020.3.1 add() also re-seeds when the queue exists and is empty (q.size()==0), so fix it before any delete-then-add preset. (2) cbDelete(obj, cb) on an object with no queue returns a CBUNREG warning, but uvm-core dereferences a null queue there (the lesson says so at line 832), so the sandbox must disallow that operation or flag it as 'not modelled'.

needs.where: ### What happens at a hook (lines 143-209); Push Further 'Live index' (line 833) and veto hooks (812-821)
needs.concept: What `uvm_do_callbacks` expands to: uvm_callback_iter (Annex D.1) walks one queue per object, by integer index into the live queue (uvm-core get_first/get_next), returns only enabled entries (D.1.2.2, D.1.2.4) of type CB or a subclass ($cast filter). So a delete inside a hook skips the next entry and a prepend reruns the current one. `uvm_do_callbacks_exit_on` returns VAL at the first callback that returns VAL, otherwise 1-VAL (B.4.5).
needs.interaction: An iterator stepper. The learner steps first()/next() with the itr index drawn under agt0's queue. They can toggle callback_mode per entry, insert an entry that is not a drv_cb (a report catcher in the pool queue) to see the type filter skip it, and pick a hook action (none / delete the next entry / prepend a new one). They predict which callbacks run, then step. An exit_on tab sets each callback's return bit; the learner predicts which callbacks are called and what the function returns.

needs.where: ### Switching callbacks at run time (lines 270-303)
needs.concept: callback_mode(0/1) is a bit on the callback object, so it affects every queue that holds it, and get_all()/display() still list it (OFF). delete(obj, cb) removes it from one queue, and re-adding puts it at the back or front, not where it was. A shared object also shares counters across drivers.

needs.where: Switching timing diagram (lines 285-301) and Push Further 'item-accurate run-time toggling' (839-847)
needs.concept: With get_next_item and then item_done after driving, a toggle between sequence calls is exact. With get() or a pipelined driver, item_done happens inside get(), so the test's callback_mode(0) and the driver's hook for the boundary item run in the same time slot in either order (IEEE 1800-2023 §4.7). Counting inside the callback avoids the race.

needs.where: ### Passing data into hooks: value, ref and const ref (lines 305-352); Push Further 'ref hooks and sequence-item identity' (849-851)
needs.concept: A hook always gets a handle. By value, field writes reach the driver's packet and pkt = new() re-points only the hook's copy. By ref, pkt = new() re-points the driver's req, and the actual must have an equivalent type (§13.5.2). By const ref, the handle cannot be assigned (compile error) but the members can still be written (§6.20.6). A swapped object loses the sequence ids unless set_id_info is called (IEEE 1800.2-2020 §14.1.2.4).
needs.interaction: The learner picks the direction and a hook statement (pkt.crc = ~pkt.crc; pkt = new(); pkt = clone), then predicts: does it compile, which object does the driver send, does the sequence's handle still see it? The reveal re-draws the heap arrows (req, pkt, the sequence's handle), shows the compile error for the const ref case, and for a swap shows the missing ids.

needs.where: ### Callbacks or a factory override? (lines 354-401)
needs.concept: Choosing the extension mechanism. A factory override chooses which class is built at create() (type or instance override, §8.3.1.4.1-2). A callback changes what runs at an existing hook, per instance, stackable and switchable at run time. A new item field needs an item type override. With no hook, subclass or ask the VIP owner. The two compose: an override can add a hook that callbacks then use.

For each of 6 to 8 cards (the scenario table's rows plus two new ones, e.g. 'one agent, 200 items mid-test, encrypted VIP' and 'replace the run_phase protocol'), the learner predicts the mechanism: instance callback, type-wide callback, factory type override, instance override, item type override, or knob/sequence field. Each card reveals why the other choices fail, and a final 'compose' card shows an override that adds a hook plus a callback on it.

Lines 31-62, Build Your Mental Model up to the first table (~670 words, the longest wall in the core path): the how-to-read note; an 8-term glossary (agent, active/passive, analysis port, virtual sequence/sequencer, configuration object, phase, objection, elaboration/time slot, parent/default sequencer); the I-UVM-3B recap (child.start() ordering, p_sequencer vs start(null), the uvm_virtual_sequencer typedef); and the dma_stream DUT's behaviour (APB setup/access, CTRL.EN and MODE, the silent drop while EN = 0, 2-cycle latency, irq after every 4th item until irq_ack), all told in prose.

Lines 107-118 (~315 words): 'What the picture shows', the two classic mistakes (a sequence on a passive agent's null handle; an active agent on DUT-driven pins, which gives X on a net or an error on a variable, IEEE 1800-2023 §6.5), and the opening of 'Configuring the topology from the test' (the is_active member vs get_is_active(), §13.4.2.2).

Lines 164-171 (~300 words): build-time configuration pitfalls. A missing set() gives NO_CFG, while a set() of a null object makes get() return 1 with cfg == null and crashes with a simulator null error. Also covers the path typo and set-before-create, then leads into the agent-count snippet.

Lines 228-238 (~305 words): the vertical-reuse debrief plus 'What changes, and what does not' (internal agents go passive, configuration nests, block virtual sequences are reused as children, block scoreboards become internal checkers).

Lines 339-352 (~295 words): 'What breaks when an environment is instantiated twice' (the ch* wildcard, a global event key, a static member, a type vs an instance override, reports with no path), the reusability rule, and the opening of 'Ordering stimulus across agents'.

Lines 377-387 (~300 words): the note that the passive case behaves differently with `this`, the long 'Reset in the middle of traffic' paragraph that walks through all three reset-handling outcomes in prose, and the quiesce/reprogram/resume intro.

Lines 420-431 (~360 words): the dout row note, the concurrent reconfiguration form, the M5 milestone and mutant definition, and the two lock rules (a grab() with no argument locks v_sqr; the holder's descendants pass is_blocked()/is_child()).

Lines 564-574 (~315 words): design rules for cross-agent checking (follow the configuration from the bus, ORDER vs MISSING, write() order within one edge is undefined per IEEE 1800-2023 §4.7, end-of-test accounting) and the per-agent vs shared intro.
Lines 1395-1425 (~540 words): the 'Run it' note, the 10 steps of 'How to build any multi-agent environment', the 7-item checklist, and the start of Push Further.

Lines 1432-1496 (~1690 words, the largest wall): seven Push Further expert sections with no visual. Lock/grab across a virtual sequence (descendants, nested holders §15.3.2.9, SEQFINERR, a grab does not pre-empt); uvm_event as a state (reset(0) strands waiters, wait_ptrigger only within one slot, pool keys are created on lookup); barriers with changing membership (threshold 0, auto-reset, lowering the threshold, cancel, reset wakeup=1 by default); ending background traffic (wait fork, disable fork, kill/m_kill, process guards, default sequence); who may object (§14.2.4.4 NOTE, starting phase, kills and objections, drain); configuration at scale; reuse at scale.
Lines 1862-1893 (~490 words, mostly reference lists, low priority): More practice plus References & Next Topics.

Borderline (under 300 words but long): lines 271-282 horizontal-reuse intro (~250); lines 611-623 rules behind the check-placement table plus the hang intro (~250); lines 517-524 event rules plus the barrier paragraph (~205).

needs.where: ### What reset does to a transfer in flight → ### The reset-aware driver → ### The reset-aware monitor → ### Flushing the scoreboard (lines 106-303)
needs.concept: Reset is a bench-wide event. At the reset edge each component holds some state and must react: the driver gives its item back with item_done() and waits for release, the monitor discards a transfer whose response edge sees reset and publishes rst_ap, and the scoreboard checks what completed, then clears model[] to the spec's 00. The core misconception: pending expectations survive reset.
needs.interaction: New MidTestResetLab on a pure src/lib/mem-reset-model.ts. The model encodes the lesson's mem_dut rule table (accept only at an edge with rst_n sampled 1; a response edge in reset aborts the transfer; reset clears memory and rdata to 00) and the page's drv/mon/sb code. Learner controls: rst_edge as a slider over mem_wr_rd_seq's 32 back-to-back requests (default 24, which reproduces the 235/245 ns trace), driver (release with item_done / drop without item_done), monitor (discard pending / publish pending), scoreboard (flush on rst_ap / no flush, the kata's bench P). Predict first which lines appear (DRV_RESET, MON_RESET, SCB_RESET, SCB_MISMATCH on the first reads after reset, 'Get_next_item called twice', SQRBADITMDN) and which post-reset reads match. Then scrub edge by edge on a CycleWaveform (clk, rst_n, valid, we, addr, rdata, err) with state cards: the driver's held item, the sequencer request FIFO, the monitor's pending, the scoreboard's 16-cell model strip and item_fifo, and rst_ap events. Highlight the active line of the driver/monitor code. needs.where: Adapter settings that move the mirror (lines 145-155, text-heavy)
needs.concept: provides_responses decides where read data comes from. With 0, the map calls bus2reg(bus_req); with 1, it blocks in get_base_response() and then calls bus2reg(bus_rsp) (uvm_reg_map.svh). If the flag does not match the driver, either read() hangs, or read() returns the request's stale data while the explicit predictor learns the real DUT value, so the next mirror(UVM_CHECK) blames the DUT. If bus2reg reports UVM_NOT_OK, the access is not predicted (PREDICT_NOK in uvm_reg::do_predict).

The model then highlights the path the map took and shows the outcome: a hang, wrong rdata with a mismatch blamed on the DUT, or a PREDICT_NOK warning.

needs.concept: Why exactly one side may wait. If a source waits for READY while a legal destination waits for VALID, the waits form a loop and nothing moves. A master that holds WVALID until AWREADY deadlocks against a legal slave that waits for WVALID before AWREADY, and the bug stays hidden against permissive slaves (IHI0022E §A3.2.1, §A3.3.1 Caution).

textHeavy: Quick Take through Words you need first (lines 17-46, about 840 words; only <BeforeYouStart />, a prerequisites line, sits between them, and there is no visual until the signal table at line 54). Covers what APB is and why it matters, the service-counter analogy and where it breaks, the four objectives, the reading roadmap, and a glossary: requester/completer, transfer, the sampled value at edge k, wait state, byte lane, agent parts, SVA operators and RAL terms.

One write and one read Debrief, then The error response: PSLVERR, then No bursts, no overlap, then APB4 PSTRB (lines 131-164, about 760 words; no visual until the PPROT table at line 168). Covers which request signals stay frozen in a wait state (the write list differs from the read list), why PREADY means nothing outside ACCESS, a read that completes with an error and invalid PRDATA, unbounded wait states, the PENABLE-rise misconception, the five PSLVERR rules (valid only at completion, recommended low elsewhere, an errored write may still have changed the register, optional, bridge mapping), no bursts vs back-to-back transfers, and PSTRB sparse writes and tie-offs.

APB4 PPROT paragraph plus APB5: wake-up, user signals, parity and RME (lines 174-183, about 285 words before the Table B-1 table; just under the 300 threshold). Covers the main use of PPROT and when a requester without PPROT can connect, then PWAKEUP rules and the deadlock risk, user signals, parity check signals, and PNSE for RME.

The skip-SETUP Debrief plus The monitor: one new item per completed transfer (lines 294-303, about 250 words; borderline). Explains why a requester that skips SETUP silences the monitor and leaves the mirror stale, then gives the monitor's three-step algorithm (SETUP edge, wait count, publish at completion), why it creates a new object per transfer, and why it catches back-to-back transfers that a PSEL-fall monitor misses.

Expected output 'How to read it', then How to build an APB agent, step by step, the checklist and the Expert back-to-back intro (lines 1070-1104, about 770 words between the log block and the zero-idle driver snippet). Covers the verdict, the timing of the seven completions (55 to 255 ns), the sparse-write result and the mirror, the ignored error, which cover properties are hit and which are not, the nine build steps and the nine-item checklist.

Expert back-to-back explanation, then Expert: what PSLVERR means for the register mirror, then Expert: byte enables in uvm-core register prediction, then the PPROT intro (lines 1123-1146, about 720 words). This is the lesson's densest uvm-core material and it has no picture. Covers the try_next_item NBA-region window, the Re-NBA last-value rule, the cycle count for 16 writes, do_predict skipping on UVM_NOT_OK (PREDICT_NOK), a pre_predict override vs post_predict, bridge error mapping, the predictor's all-lanes byte_en default, the lowest-byte-lane field rule and is_indv_accessible.

PPROT null-test paragraph, then Expert: APB5 in a VIP, then Expert: recommendations are not rules (lines 1181-1193, about 450 words before the interview widgets). Covers the $cast and null rule, the PWAKEUP, user-signal, parity and RME checks a VIP must add, issue C vs issue E recommendations, and the wait bound as testbench policy.

Kata worked solution, steps 3-5 (lines 1479-1483, about 310 words of prose after the code). Covers the expected silence plus the WAIT_STATS evidence, Mutant A (a_wait_hold fails one edge after the first wait state, zero-wait transfers hide the bug, and the DUT writes addr+4 while the monitor reports addr) and Mutant B (a_wait_bound is policy, not protocol).

needs.where: Three states: IDLE, SETUP, ACCESS + One write and one read, edge by edge (lines 71-138)
needs.concept: An APB transfer as a three-state machine. SETUP lasts exactly one cycle with PENABLE low. ACCESS repeats while PREADY is low. The transfer completes at the first edge where PSEL, PENABLE and PREADY are all 1. Wait states are counted correctly: SETUP is not a wait state, and PREADY outside ACCESS is ignored.
needs.interaction: The learner picks a preset: the lesson's write with one wait state followed by a read ending in PSLVERR, a zero-wait read, or N wait states. They set the completer's PREADY for each ACCESS edge on an editable CycleWaveform (keyboard toggles). They predict the completion edge and the number of wait states by choosing an edge, then step with the scrubber. At each edge the IDLE/SETUP/ACCESS state picture lights the current state, and markers label SETUP, wait and completion. Narration gives What and Why with the IHI 0024C clause (§4.1, §3.1.2, §3.3.2). PREADY values outside ACCESS are greyed and labelled 'ignored' (§3.1.2: any value when PENABLE is LOW).

needs.concept: The adapter maps PSLVERR to UVM_NOT_OK. uvm_reg::do_predict skips prediction with a PREDICT_NOK warning for any status other than UVM_IS_OK. needs.where: ### Address phase and data phase (lines 108-130)
needs.concept: The two-stage pipeline: a transfer's address is accepted at one edge and its data at the next HREADY-high edge, and the next address phase overlaps the current data phase. Read the waveform diagonally, not down one column (§3.1; misconception 1 in the spine card).
needs.interaction: The learner predicts the edge at which A's write data is sampled (edge 1 or edge 2), then steps cycle by cycle. Tokens A and B sit in two slots, 'Address phase' and 'Data phase'. At every HREADY-high edge A moves into the data slot as B enters the address slot, and an arrow joins HADDR=A (edge 1) to Data A (edge 2), so the diagonal pairing is drawn instead of described.

It also has no pipeline-stage view: add a two-slot stage strip and edge-to-edge pairing arrows, both read from the same AhbTrace cycle (dataPhase, acceptEdge and completeEdge already exist in BeatRecord).

needs.where: ### Wait states: HREADY low holds both phases (lines 132-161)
needs.concept: One HREADY releases both pipeline stages. A wait state on A holds A's data phase and B's address phase, so a driver that advances while HREADY is low drops a transfer (§3.1, Figure 3-5, §3.6; misconception 2 in the spine card).
needs.interaction: The learner sets the wait states on A (0 to 3) and predicts the edge where B's address is accepted and the edge where Data B is sampled. Stepping through, both stage slots show a hold glyph on every HREADY-low cycle and release together. A 'driver ignores HREADY' toggle then replaces B while HREADY is low: B vanishes from the ledger and the existing hold-in-wait property fails at that edge.

needs.where: ### Where AHB sits: master, decoder, multiplexor (lines 43-80), plus Push Further 'Expert: HSELx timing and the retimed multiplexor select' (lines 630-632)
needs.concept: The interconnect. The decoder raises one HSELx from HADDR in the address phase. The multiplexor routes the data-phase slave's HRDATA/HRESP/HREADYOUT, so its select must be retimed to the data phase (§2.4 Note). One HREADY fans out to the master and every slave. The default slave answers NONSEQ/SEQ with ERROR and IDLE/BUSY with a zero-wait OKAY (§4.2.1).
needs.interaction: The learner picks a sequence: A to S2 at 0x400 with 2 waits, then B to S1 at 0x040; a NONSEQ to an unmapped address; or an IDLE to an unmapped address. Stepping through cycles, a block view lights HSELx at the decoder in the address phase and the registered mux select one transfer later, shows each slave's HREADYOUT, and shows the single HREADY going back to the master and to every slave. Predictions to answer: 'In cycle 3, whose HREADYOUT is on HREADY?' and 'What does the default slave answer to this IDLE and to this NONSEQ?'. A toggle switches the mux select between 'retimed to data phase' and 'combinational from HSELx (bug)'; with the bug, the mux routes S1's HREADYOUT and HRESP while S2 still owns the data phase.
needs.existing: ArchitectureDiagram (static, line 54). AhbPipelineBurstVisualizer covers one slave region only.
needs.gap: src/lib/ahb-model.ts models one slave region and has no HSELx, decoder, multiplexor or default slave ('Illegal bursts are flagged, not routed to a second slave'). New src/lib/ahb-interconnect-model.ts, reusing simulateAhb timing, with: an address map (S1 0x000-0x3FF, S2 0x400-0x7FF, default slave elsewhere), HREADYOUT/HRESP per slave, a registered mux select with a fault switch, and default-slave responses. New component AhbInterconnectExplorer, drawn with BlockDiagram plus CycleWaveform. The same model would also serve B-AHB-2 ('Retiming the multiplexor select to the data phase') and B-AHB-3 ('Where HREADY comes from').

needs.where: ### When a slave samples: HSELx and HREADY (lines 163-189)
needs.concept: HSELx says which slave the address phase is for, and HREADY says whether the bus moves. A slave samples HSELx, address and control only when HREADY is high. HSELx is combinational and can be high during a wait for a transfer that is not accepted yet (§4.2, Table 2-4).
needs.interaction: Uses the lesson figure's scenario: S2 holds HREADY low for two edges while the master offers IDLE 0x404 and then NONSEQ B 0x040 to S1. The learner chooses S1's design, 'registers when HSEL_S1 && HREADY' or 'registers whenever HSEL_S1', and predicts at which edge or edges S1 registers B. The run shows the naive slave registering B at edge 3, while S2 still owns the data phase, and again at edge 4 (a double count); the correct slave registers B once, at edge 4. It also shows HSEL_S2 high at edge 2 for an IDLE that S2 ignores.

needs.where: ### Transfer types: IDLE, BUSY, NONSEQ, SEQ (lines 191-234)
needs.concept: Legal HTRANS sequences. BUSY only between beats, with address and control showing the next beat. A SINGLE must be followed by IDLE or NONSEQ. A fixed-length burst must end with SEQ. An undefined-length INCR may end with BUSY, then NONSEQ or IDLE. A burst starts with NONSEQ. Masters may not end a burst early (§3.2 Table 3-1, §3.5.1, §3.5.2). Also BUSY (the master pausing) vs a wait state (the slave stretching).
needs.interaction: The learner picks HBURST (SINGLE, INCR, INCR4 or WRAP4) and taps IDLE/BUSY/NONSEQ/SEQ tiles to compose the cycles, then predicts legal or illegal before checking. The model marks the first illegal cycle with its rule and clause, for example 'BUSY immediately after a SINGLE', 'fixed-length burst ends with BUSY', 'burst starts with SEQ', or 'INCR4 stopped after 3 beats with no ERROR'. A legal sequence then plays as a short waveform in which every BUSY gets a zero-wait OKAY and HTRANS[1] marks the real transfers.

needs.where: ### Bursts: HBURST, HSIZE and beat addresses (lines 236-287); kata items 1, 2 and 4 (lines 845-848)
needs.concept: Beat-address arithmetic. Incrementing bursts add 2^HSIZE each beat. Wrapping bursts stay inside an aligned block of beats × size bytes and fold back to the block base. Every beat must be aligned to its size. Misconception: a WRAP8 of words from 0x34 does not wrap at 0x30 (§3.4 Table 3-2, §3.5 Table 3-3, Figures 3-8 to 3-11).
needs.interaction: The learner picks HBURST (all eight types, with a beat count for INCR), HSIZE (byte, halfword or word) and a start address. Presets: WRAP8 of words from 0x34 (Figure 3-10), WRAP4 of words from 0x34, WRAP4 from 0x38 (Figure 3-8), INCR8 of halfwords from 0x34 (Figure 3-11), and custom. The learner predicts the beat that follows 0x3C (0x40, 0x30 or 0x20). The reveal places numbered beats on an address ruler with the beats × size block shaded and a fold-back arrow at the wrap, and shows the per-beat formula rows (addr + size, & (block − 1), base | low bits) exactly like the lesson's traced table. An unaligned start is flagged with §3.5.

needs.where: ### The 1KB rule (lines 289-318); kata item 3; Push Further 'Expert: can a legal burst span two slave regions?' (lines 634-636)
needs.concept: Masters must not start an incrementing burst (including undefined-length INCR) that crosses 1KB, because slave regions are at least 1KB and start and end on 1KB boundaries. WRAP bursts are exempt because they never leave their block. The fix is a new NONSEQ at the 1KB address. Contrast with the AXI 4KB rule. Corner case: a WRAP16 of 1024-bit beats has a 2KB block that spans two 1KB regions (§3.5, §4.2; misconception 3 in the spine card).
needs.interaction: On an address map with S1 (0x000-0x3FF) and S2 (0x400-0x7FF) and a fence at 0x400, the learner moves the start address toward 0x3F8 for INCR4/8/16 or INCR of n beats and predicts whether the burst is legal and which beat crosses. The reveal colours each beat by the slave that owns it: S1 loses its last beats and S2's first transfer is a SEQ. A 'split legally' control re-issues the remainder as a NONSEQ at 0x400. Switching to WRAP4 at 0x3F8 shows the burst staying in 0x3F0-0x3FF. A bus-width control unlocks the WRAP16 × 1024-bit case.

needs.where: ### Responses: OKAY, wait states and the two-cycle ERROR (lines 320-361)
needs.concept: How the HREADYOUT × HRESP combinations encode a response (Table 5-2). ERROR takes two cycles because the next address is already on the bus, and in the second cycle the master either cancels with IDLE or continues (§5.1.3, §3.5.2). ERROR read data is not valid (§6.1.2).
needs.interaction: The learner sets 'cancels' or 'continues' and the number of OKAY waits before the ERROR, with A as an INCR4 that errors on its second beat, matching the lesson figure. Before stepping, the learner predicts HTRANS in the second ERROR cycle and whether SEQ 0x48 is accepted. During playback, a 2×2 HREADYOUT × HRESP grid lights the cell for the current cycle (wait, then ERROR first cycle, then ERROR second cycle), and the ledger marks 0x48 as cancelled or accepted.

needs.where: ### In your testbench (lines 428-472): the monitor rule, the run_phase snippet and the 9-row symptom → cause → fix table
needs.concept: The monitor rule: an address phase is accepted at an HREADY-high edge with HTRANS[1] = 1 (plus HSELx for a slave-side monitor), and its data and response are taken at the next HREADY-high edge. At one edge the monitor closes the old transfer before opening the new one. The driver holds NONSEQ/SEQ until HREADY is high. Each debugging-table row is one violation of this rule.
needs.interaction: The learner picks a trace (wait states, BUSY burst, ERROR read) and a monitor variant: correct; ignores HREADY; pairs address and data at the same edge; counts BUSY as a transfer; captures HRDATA in a wait cycle; compares HRDATA on ERROR. The learner then predicts which reported transactions will be wrong. Stepping edge by edge highlights the executing line of the lesson's monitor loop (CodeTrace) and shows pend_valid and pend, and an expected-vs-actual ledger marks each reported transaction ✓ or ✕ with the debugging-table row that explains it.

needs.where: ## Make It Work, 'How to read any AHB waveform, in six steps' (lines 601-607), and the Lab predictions run-list (lines 862-864)
needs.concept: The six-step waveform-reading procedure as a retrieval skill: mark the HREADY-high edges, find the accepted NONSEQ/SEQ, pair each with its data at the next marked edge, classify each HREADY-low edge as a wait state or the first ERROR cycle, check burst addresses, and check the second ERROR cycle and cancel vs continue.
needs.interaction: A seeded trace (a mix of waits, a BUSY, a burst and possibly an ERROR) appears with no markers. needs.concept: Pipelining puts B's address on the bus before the slave answers A. The first ERROR cycle (HREADY low) stops B from being accepted, so the master can drive IDLE in the second cycle to cancel it, or continue (§5.1.3, §3.5.2). A one-cycle ERROR lets B be accepted at the same edge the master learns of the error.

needs.where: ### Pitfall 5: locks that starve other masters, SequenceDiagram + lock counter + TimingDiagram (L372-463)
needs.concept: A locked sequence must be processed before any other transfer (§3.3), so other masters wait for the whole lock, wait states included. That is bounded starvation, not deadlock. The lock lasts from a cycle with HMASTLOCK and HREADY high until a cycle with HMASTLOCK low and HREADY high (IHI0033C §3.3), so a counter driven by HMASTLOCK alone misses the last data phase's waits.

Bounded waits show 'starvation risk'; a lock that is never released becomes unbounded and the run ends at the test timeout. (b) Counter panel on the same edges: locked/lock_cycles vs an HMASTLOCK-only counter, with a MAX_LOCK_CYCLES slider. The learner predicts whether and when each counter warns. Reproduce the lesson's case: lock_cycles reaches 5 at edge 6; the HMASTLOCK-only counter peaks at 3. Declared fidelity assumptions: arbitration is interconnect policy (§4.1), and holding a master with HREADY low is one interconnect design (IHI0033C §4.4).

A second scenario shows HSEL_S1 high during an IDLE-address change while HREADY is low.

They predict what the monitor publishes and whether the a_hwdata_hold attempt from the waited edge passes, fails or is disabled. needs.where: ### The scoreboard (lines 334-358)
needs.concept: With no write strobes in IHI0033B.b, byte lanes come from HADDR and HSIZE (§6.2.1). The reference model stores bytes. Error policy: an ERROR read is not compared. Reads of unwritten bytes count as pending, and check_phase fails when nothing was compared (SCB_EMPTY).
needs.interaction: Learner issues writes and reads on a 32-bit bus (address, HSIZE, data, OKAY or ERROR). Before each read they predict the verdict (match, mismatch, pending, or not compared because of ERROR) and which lane carries byte 0x1001. Then active lanes light on HWDATA/HRDATA[31:0], the sparse byte map grows with each write, and the SCB_SUMMARY counters update. A 'disconnect ap' toggle shows SCB_EMPTY at check_phase. Presets: the page's traced example (byte 0xAB to 0x1001, then a word read of 0x1000, which ends pending) and the Make It Work final read 0xa000ab00.

needs.where: ### Debug patterns, 1. The HREADY trace (lines 528-555)
needs.concept: HREADY is the multiplexor's choice of the data-phase owner's HREADYOUT. The mux select is the decoder output retimed to the data phase (§2.4 Note, §4.3), and HREADY goes back to every slave, so one waiting slave stalls the whole bus.
needs.interaction: A 3-slave system stalls. The learner scrubs to the edge where HREADY fell and predicts which slave is holding it. The trap answer is the slave HADDR decodes to now, whose address phase is only waiting. The reveal lights the registered select path through the mux and the owning slave's HREADYOUT. Variants: a slave inserting waits on an IDLE, which breaks Table 3-1 (a_idle_busy_zero_wait_okay names it), and an unmapped NONSEQ answered by the default slave with ERROR while IDLE/BUSY get a zero-wait OKAY (§4.2.1).
needs.gap: New interconnect model (decoder map, data-phase select registered at HREADY-high edges, per-slave HREADYOUT and HRESP, default slave) and component (BlockDiagram + CycleWaveform + PredictionPrompt). The page today has only a static ArchitectureDiagram of Figure 4-2, and AhbPipelineBurstVisualizer models one slave.

needs.where: ### Debug patterns, 3. ERROR forensics (lines 569-596)
needs.concept: Walk back from the ERROR completion (HRESP and HREADY high) through the first ERROR cycle and any OKAY waits to the accepting edge of the failing transfer. Then read cancel vs continue from HTRANS in the second ERROR cycle (§3.5.2, §5.1.3).
needs.interaction: Forensics drill. The learner clicks the edge where the ERROR completes, then the edge that accepted the failing transfer. 'OKAY waits before ERROR' (0-2) changes the distance between them, so the drill cannot be memorised. Finally they predict whether the master cancelled or continued. A HintLadder supports each step, and wrong clicks get diagnostic feedback (for example, picking the first ERROR cycle).

needs.where: ### Stimulus side: responder Predict and Debrief (lines 379-475)
needs.concept: A responder sets the first data-phase cycle in the time step of the accepting edge k: a clocking-block drive takes effect after edge k (§14.16). A driver that waits for edge k+1 lets the transfer complete OKAY at k+1.

Predict what HREADY and HRESP are sampled at edge k+1 and which response the transfer receives. The resulting waveform shows that a late ERROR lands on the next data phase, and on an IDLE it also breaks the zero-wait OKAY rule (Table 3-1).

needs.where: ### The five channels and who drives what (lines 52-116; break up the text-heavy stretch 108-130)
needs.concept: Five one-way channels between master and slave. On each channel the source drives VALID and the information, and the destination drives READY back against the arrow. A write uses AW, W, B and a read uses AR, R. There is one B for the whole burst but an RRESP on every R beat (A1.3, A3.2.1, A3.4.4).
needs.interaction: A spatial 'lanes' view beside the waveform: five horizontal pipes from Master to Slave (B and R pointing back), each with an item token and a READY gate at the destination end. The learner scrubs edge by edge with PlaybackControls. Before stepping they answer a few predictions: which side drives BREADY and RREADY (click a side), how many B tokens a 3-beat write produces, how many RRESP chips a 3-beat read carries. Then they see tokens wait at a closed gate (stall), pass on a handshake edge, and B leave only after the AW and WLAST tokens have arrived. Clicking the BREADY gate shut for good shows BVALID stuck high forever (mistake 1 in the lesson).

LESSON_FIGURES.write and LESSON_FIGURES.read in the model already hold the lesson's 3-beat write and read.

needs.concept: The hold and stability rule applies at every stalled edge, not just after VALID rises (A3.2.1). $rose(valid) |=> $stable(info) misses a stall that follows a back-to-back transfer, and it fails falsely on legal back-to-back traffic.

needs.where: ### Why a source never waits for READY, Rule A (lines 220-244), also referenced from the Debug challenge 'the driver that waits' (1211-1263)
needs.concept: Deadlock. A destination may legally wait for VALID. If the source also waited for READY, the two would wait forever. The A3.3.1 Caution example: a master holds WVALID until AWREADY while the slave holds AWREADY until WVALID.
needs.interaction: The learner toggles which signals wait for which on the master and slave sides, predicts deadlock / latent violation / safe, and then sees the wait-for graph with every loop drawn. They start on the Caution pair, remove the illegal master wait and watch the loop break. Then they try 'Latent violation' (an illegal master wait that happens to complete against this slave).
needs.existing: AxiDeadlockSimulator (no props; it already opens on the 'Classic W/AW deadlock' preset, which is exactly the A3.3.1 Caution; other presets: Legal delayed READY, Latent violation, B-channel deadlock). It is registered for MDX and used in B-AXI-5 and B-AMBA-F3. Its assumptions limit it to one write on one interface, which fits this lesson's scope.

needs.where: ### Why a source never waits for READY, Rule B (lines 246-254) and Push Further 'combinational paths and register slices' (888-892)
needs.concept: No combinational path from any input to any output of a master or slave interface (A3.1.1, A3.2.1). The rule is symmetric: READY = f(VALID) is as illegal as VALID = f(READY). 'May wait for VALID' means across edges.
needs.interaction: Two component boxes joined by one channel. For each side the learner picks 'output registered' or 'output combinational from the input' (VALID from READY on the master, READY from VALID on the slave). They predict whether the interface is legal and whether a combinational loop closes. The diagram then traces the combinational path through the components and names A3.1.1. The 'why' (a timing loop, timing that crosses components) must carry fidelity 'illustration', because the spec gives no reason.

needs.where: ### Cross-channel dependencies (text-heavy 256-273; explorer at 274)
needs.concept: The only cross-channel rules: RVALID after the AR handshake; in AXI4, BVALID after both the AW handshake and the WLAST handshake; W may come before, with or after its AW (A3.3, A3.3.1). The spec gives the cause: W leads 'if the write address channel contains more register stages than the write data channel' (A3.3), and each register slice adds one cycle of latency (A1.3.3). This targets spine misconceptions 1 and 2.
needs.interaction: Two steppers, 'register stages on the AW path' and 'register stages on the W path'. The learner predicts which reaches the slave interface first and the earliest edge BVALID may be high, then sees the trace with the dependency-wait narration. An AXI3/AXI4 toggle shows the same early-B trace as legal under AXI3 (where B-after-AW is only strongly recommended, A3.3.2) and as an a_b_dep violation under AXI4.

needs.where: ### Channel independence and backpressure (text-heavy 315-339; the predict at 321 points to the explorer 'above')
needs.concept: A stall on one channel stops only that channel's handshakes and the channels that depend on it: W backpressure delays that write's B, never AR or R. This contrasts with AHB, where one HREADY stalls the whole pipeline.
needs.interaction: A second instance of the dependency explorer, opened directly on 'Backpressure on W only' next to the prompt. The learner predicts the RLAST edge and the B edge, then lengthens the WREADY stall by clicking cells and sees R unchanged while B slides later.
needs.existing: AxiChannelHandshakeVisualizer has the 'independent' scenario (Backpressure on W only).
needs.gap: No initialScenario prop (and no scenarios subset) to open it on 'independent' here. Without one the prompt depends on scrolling back to line 274.

needs.where: ### End-to-end write and read flows (lines 334-419) and Push Further 'responses, errors and burst completion' (911-913)
needs.concept: A complete write (AW, 3 x W, one B after AW and WLAST) and read (AR, then 3 x R each with its own RRESP). An error response does not end a burst early: all beats are still transferred, and a write can only deassert strobes (A3.4.1, A3.4.4).
needs.interaction: The lanes view from need 1, scrubbed on the lesson's write and read scenarios. Toggles: 'make the master W-first', and 'SLVERR on read beat 2'. Before revealing, the learner predicts how many R beats follow the error and which beat carries RLAST, then sees all beats still flow with RLAST on the last.

needs.where: ### Reset (text-heavy 412-432; static TimingDiagrams at 433-465; code at 469) and Push Further 'reset corner cases' (904-909)
needs.concept: The three A3.1.2 rules. ARESETn may assert asynchronously but must deassert synchronously. VALIDs are LOW during reset. A master may begin driving VALID HIGH only at an edge after the first edge with ARESETn HIGH. !ARESETn |-> !valid misses rule 3, so the $rose(ARESETn) term is needed. An edge-sampled assertion cannot see a reset pulse between edges, and disable iff uses current, not sampled, values (IEEE 1800-2023 §16.12).
needs.interaction: The learner drags the reset-release edge and the master's first AWVALID edge on a CycleWaveform. They predict legal or illegal, and which of the two reset properties catches it, then see the result. A 'glitch' toggle inserts an asynchronous reset pulse between two edges: the learner predicts whether p_reset sees it, then sees that no sampled edge observes it.
needs.gap: axi-channel-model.ts states 'Reset is not modelled'. It needs an ARESETn row and the A3.1.2 rules 2 and 3 in checkChannels, plus a reset focus or scenarios in AxiChannelHandshakeVisualizer, or a small dedicated component.

needs.where: ### In a real testbench, the master-driver bullet and drive_aw explanation (lines 497-511, text-heavy 511-516)
needs.concept: A clocking drive issued between clocking events matures at the next clocking event (IEEE 1800-2023 §14.16). Two drives maturing in the same Re-NBA region: the last one wins (§14.16.2). So drive_aw must start right after @(vif.cb), or the item is lost without a transfer.
needs.interaction: Step through drive_aw against a slave. The learner picks 'called right after @(vif.cb)' or 'called mid-cycle' and when AWREADY rises. They predict whether 0x1000 transfers and at which edge AWVALID falls. The timeline then shows each drive's issue time, the clocking event where it matures, the do-while loop's sampled AWREADY, and in the mid-cycle case AWVALID <= 0 overriding AWVALID <= 1 in the same time step.
needs.existing: ClockingBlockSkewVisualizer (model src/lib/sv-clocking-model.ts) covers input and output skew and the drive statement form on a timeline. TimeSlotTraceVisualizer covers tb-clocking-block region ordering.
needs.gap: ClockingBlockSkewVisualizer has no 'drive issued between clocking events' scenario and no 'two drives mature in the same Re-NBA, last wins' scenario. It would need both, plus an AWREADY-driven loop, to show this idiom.

needs.where: ### In a real testbench, the monitor bullet (line 513), with mistake 'Assuming AW always arrives before W' (VisualRecap 291), interview 'writes lost under random backpressure' (971-980) and debugging-table row 3
needs.concept: A monitor must collect W in its own thread, queue W bursts, and pair them with AW items in AW order (A3.3, A5.4.1). A monitor that collects W only after it has seen AW drops data that arrives first, and this shows up only under random READY.
needs.interaction: A seeded random READY policy generates several writes with mixed AW/W orders. The learner picks a monitor design ('W only after AW' or 'per-channel queues') and predicts how many writes reach the scoreboard intact. Then they watch the AW queue and W queue fill and pair, and see the buggy design drop the early W bursts.
needs.existing: ScoreboardMatchingVisualizer (src/lib/scoreboard-model.ts) teaches in-order vs per-ID scoreboard queues, not AW/W pairing in a monitor.
needs.gap: No AW/W pairing model. It needs a small pure function (W-burst queue plus AW queue, in-order pairing) and a view. Overlaps B-AXI-6 (VIP and monitors), so it could live there and be embedded here.

needs.concept: How the counter-based checker sees the tb_top trace. Counters sampled in Preponed (§16.5.1) count only earlier edges, which is why a B on the AW handshake edge fails a_b_dep. Each plusarg mutation fails exactly one assertion at one edge.
needs.interaction: A checker trace lab loaded with tb_top's *_V arrays. The learner picks the legal run or a mutation (+BROKEN_B, +BROKEN_W, +BROKEN_RST, +BROKEN_R; the kata's KATA_WDATA and KATA_LATE_AW behind a 'kata: attempt first' gate). They predict the failing assertion and edge, then scrub edges: the five counters aw_done...rlast_done show their sampled values under the cursor, mutated cells are highlighted, and the firing assertion lights up in the CodeTrace. This replaces the hand-traced expected output with a model check.

needs.where: Push Further, Expert: combinational paths and register slices (lines 888-892, inside text-heavy 888-919)
needs.concept: Each register slice adds one cycle of latency on its channel (A1.3.3). A naive slice that registers READY halves throughput, while a two-entry skid buffer keeps one transfer per edge. The slice designs are common design practice, not spec.
needs.interaction: The learner inserts a slice on one channel and picks 'naive (registered READY)' or 'skid buffer'. They predict how many transfers get through in 8 edges with VALID held high and READY always high downstream. Then they see per-side handshakes and buffer occupancy edge by edge. Fidelity: 'model' for the latency (spec), 'illustration' (or a model of a design) for the two slice designs.
needs.gap: New pure model needed, e.g. src/lib/axi-register-slice-model.ts, with naive and skid-buffer slices driven by the existing ChannelScenario conventions.

needs.where: Push Further, Expert: default READY values and their obligations (lines 894-898) and throughput (937-939)
needs.concept: AWREADY and ARREADY may default HIGH or LOW, and HIGH is recommended. A default of LOW forces at least two cycles per transfer. A default-HIGH WREADY, BREADY or RREADY is allowed only if that side can always accept in one cycle (A3.2.2).
needs.interaction: In the handshake explorer, a 'slave READY policy' control: default HIGH (always) or default LOW (raise READY one edge after seeing VALID). The learner predicts the cycles per address for 3 back-to-back addresses, then sees the waveform and a cycles-per-transfer readout.

needs.concept: Wrap_Boundary = INT(start/(Number_Bytes x Burst_Length)) x total. The upper limit is never used as an address. The burst wraps at most once. A WRAP that starts on its boundary never wraps. WRAP must start aligned and have 2, 4, 8 or 16 transfers.

needs.where: ### The 4KB rule (lines 376-467), in the text-heavy stretch 368-390 and after the fence SVG at 405
needs.concept: Count the last byte from the aligned start. Only INCR can cross 4KB. A checker that uses AxADDR + total bytes, or that is not gated on INCR, fails legal bursts. These are misconceptions 2 and 4 and the debug-table rows 2-3.

needs.concept: Relational operands are sized to max(L(i),L(j)) (IEEE 1800-2023 Table 11-21). With every operand 12 bits, the carry out of bit 11 (which is the crossing itself) is lost, and the constraint is always true.

needs.where: Outstanding transactions: 'Why outstanding transactions exist' and 'Outstanding depth is a design parameter' (L75-77), reused in Push Further 'Expert: sizing outstanding depth and ID width' (L702-706) and the 'how many outstanding reads?' interview question
needs.concept: Outstanding depth hides latency: R-channel utilisation grows with N until R is full, and N >= (L + B) / B with L measured to the first beat (Little's law, which the lesson labels a queueing estimate, not a rule of the spec). The slave applies backpressure by holding ARREADY low when full. IHI0022E sets no maximum, and the read data reordering depth is static and cannot be discovered (A5.3.1).
needs.interaction: Sliders: latency to first beat L, beats per burst B, master outstanding limit N, slave acceptance limit. The learner first predicts the smallest N that keeps R busy (or the utilisation for the chosen N). Then a cycle timeline shows AR issues, ARREADY held low when the slave is full, one slot bar per outstanding read (L + B cycles) and R-channel occupancy, with utilisation %. Presets: 'one at a time' (N=1, R idle ~100 cycles), 'L=100, B=16' (answer 8, matching the interview question), 'slave accepts only 4' (backpressure caps throughput). Fidelity badge 'model' with stated assumptions: fixed latency, one beat per cycle, in-order slave.
