A monitor-bug toggle ('pair with the AW nearest in time' / 'W before AW is an error') re-runs the same legal trace and shows the wrong pairing. needs.where: The interconnect: ID extension, routing (L319-352), and Push Further 'ID width growth' (L708)
needs.concept: The interconnect appends master-port bits (A5.3.5); this lesson places them above the master's bits, which is an implementation choice. The slave therefore sees a wider ID, and responses are routed by those bits and stripped on the way back. Cascaded interconnects add bits at each level (recommended widths per A5.3.6). A slave ID port that is too narrow misroutes responses.

A bit strip then grows level by level, with master bits and port bits in different colours. Pressing 'respond' plays the return path: each level routes by its bits and strips them. A fault toggle, 'slave ID port one bit too narrow', truncates the top bit and the response lands at the wrong master.

needs.concept: Response order at the master is always issue order for same-ID, same-direction transactions. Arrival order at the slave is guaranteed for Device memory (to one slave, whatever the address) and for Normal memory only at the same or overlapping addresses (A6.2, A4.3.2). Slave observation obligations follow from this (A6.4). A read and a write are never ordered without waiting for the response.

textHeavy: Lines 19-61 (Quick Take, 'You will be able to', 'How to read this lesson', 'Words you need first'): about 1,000 words. The only thing between them is <BeforeYouStart />, which is not a teaching visual. Covers the four attributes, the parcel analogy and 14 glossary terms: response codes with encodings, intermediate point, Device vs Normal, write-through vs write-back, cacheable, privileged/Secure, semaphore, arbiter, UNPREDICTABLE.

Lines 161-182 (AxPROT bullets, the 'Predict first' prompt with its <details> answer, the first two AxQOS paragraphs): about 345 words, broken only by the details reveal. Covers bit-1 polarity, how privilege levels map, the instruction bit as a hint, AxPROT never being changed, refusal response as system policy, the 4-bit QoS identifier, 0000 = not participating, interconnect overwrite, and the default rule that ordering wins.

Lines 205-221 (AxQOS 'Why bother?' paragraph, then 'Exclusive access: the flow' steps 1-7): about 400 words. Covers display underflow and why QoS is not a latency guarantee, then the exclusive read, the monitor recording address and ID, EXOKAY vs OKAY on the read, the write-after-read rule, the monitor's decision, and LDREX/STREX retry.

Lines 246-268 (visualizer Debrief bullets plus 'Exclusive access: rules and corner cases'): about 550 words. Covers race outcomes for each monitor policy, what a slave without support does, the bad-shape debrief, the five A7.2.4 restrictions, why an unpaired exclusive write is legal, the pin-checkable write-after-read rule, spurious failures from a monitored block larger than the access (up to 128 bytes), and interconnect ID extension.

Lines 279-308 (end of locked transfers, 'Global and local monitors', 'Pitfalls and misconceptions' 1-7, 'In a real testbench' bullets): about 505 words. Covers the AXI3 locked-to-normal conversion, local vs global monitor, the seven misconceptions, and what the item, driver, monitor, scoreboard, assertions and coverage each own.

Lines 672-712 (note on covering exclusive outcomes, 'How to verify the attributes of an AXI port' steps 1-9, the checklist, Push Further 'what an interconnect may legally change', the first two paragraphs of 'buffering, early responses and proof of arrival'): about 760 words. Covers the verification plan, the Non-modifiable / Modifiable / never-allowed change rules with their exceptions, and early-response obligations.

Lines 733-767 ('mismatched and changing memory attributes', 'exclusive monitors in real systems', 'single-copy and multi-copy atomicity', 'AxREGION and AxUSER', 'AXI5 atomic transactions' bullets): about 1,140 words, the longest stretch in the lesson. Atomicity and mismatched attributes are each one dense paragraph of over 170 words. The AXI5 part is seven bullets on forms, AWATOP, sizes, responses, IDs and support.

needs.where: ### AxCACHE bit by bit (AXI4 names) + ### The twelve memory types (lines 72-142, replacing nothing; sits before the existing ArchitectureDiagram)
needs.concept: Decoding a 4-bit AxCACHE value, per channel, into a Table A4-5 memory type and the permissions that type grants (§A4.4.1): early write response from an intermediate point, merge/split/fetch-more (Modifiable, §A4.3.1), mandatory cache lookup when AxCACHE[3:2] != 00 (§A4.3.3), read data from a cached copy or prefetch. Also covers the six reserved values (an allocate bit without Modifiable) and the fact that the same type has different encodings on AR and AW (Write-through No-allocate is 1010 on AR, 0110 on AW).
needs.interaction: The learner flips an AR/AW channel switch and toggles the four bits, or picks a preset: register poll 0000, doorbell 0001, frame buffer 0011, WT No-allocate on both channels, AXI3 legacy 0110 on AR, reserved 0100. Before the reveal they commit to (a) legal or reserved, (b) the memory type, (c) checkboxes: 'write buffer may send B', 'may merge or split', 'must be looked up in a cache', 'read may come from a cached copy or be prefetched'. The reveal lights the master -> write buffer -> system cache -> final destination path. It shows who may answer and whether the transaction may change shape, and cites the Table A4-5 row and §A4.4.1 requirement. Every wrong checkbox gets misconception feedback, such as the AXI3-name trap for bit 3 on AR. A second drill runs in reverse: given a memory type, set the bits for AR and then for AW. A 4x4 legality grid for each channel shows the six reserved cells hatched.

needs.where: ### Pitfall: a register mapped with the wrong AxCACHE (lines 144-150), also backs quiz Q1
needs.concept: Why registers with side effects need a Device type. Normal memory permits the system to serve two polls from one fetch, widen a read onto a neighbouring FIFO register, or answer from a stale cached copy. None of this is a protocol violation (§A4.3.1, §A4.4.1).
needs.interaction: Build this as a 'What may the system do to this register?' mode of the AxCACHE explorer from need 1. The learner picks AxCACHE (0000, 0001, 0010, 0011, 1111) for a status-poll loop and for a UART RX FIFO read. They predict whether every poll is guaranteed to reach the peripheral, and whether a FIFO byte can be popped that software never read. The reveal steps through each transformation the type permits: merged polls, a widened read, a hit on a stale copy. Each step is labelled 'permitted, not required' with its clause. Device types show none of them.

needs.where: ### AxPROT: who is asking (lines 152-175)
needs.concept: Three independent AxPROT bits (Table A4-6) and the inverted bit 1 (1 = Non-secure). AxPROT is never changed on the way (§A4.3.1). The reaction to a refused access is system policy, not AXI.
needs.interaction: The learner gets three scenario cards: a Non-secure kernel data read, Secure privileged firmware fetching instructions, and a Non-secure user write. For each they set AxPROT[2:0] with toggles and commit before the reveal. A 'VIP drives AxPROT[1]=1 for secure' trap card asks them to predict what happens to every Secure access. A firewall in front of a Secure and a Non-secure region then shows pass or refuse. The refusal response is shown as 'system policy, e.g. SLVERR or DECERR', with fidelity 'illustration' for the firewall and 'model' for the Table A4-6 encoding. Could be a tab of the need-1 component.

needs.where: ### AxQOS: a priority hint (lines 177-206, next to the existing SequenceDiagram)
needs.concept: QoS picks among waiting transactions only where no AXI ordering rule fixes the order (§A8.1.3). 0000 means not participating (§A8.1.1). An interconnect may overwrite the values (§A8.1.2). Same-ID read data still returns in order (§A5.3.1). QoS is not a latency guarantee.
needs.interaction: Display and GPU reads queue at an arbiter. The learner sets each ARQOS, chooses same or different ARID, and toggles 'interconnect overwrites QoS from its registers' and 'arbiter honours QoS'. They predict the order of R data, then play the slave. The model rejects any order that breaks same-ID ordering and marks the beat a QoS-honouring arbiter would pick. Key moment: R2 at QoS 15 cannot overtake R1 at QoS 4 with the same ID, but can once the IDs differ. Any latency readout is marked as an illustration.

needs.where: ### Exclusive access: rules and corner cases (lines 252-268), the text-heavy debrief at 246-251, and the embed at line 245
needs.concept: How the monitor behaves in the cases the prose explains but the visualizer cannot show. An exclusive write with no prior exclusive read is legal and fails with OKAY, memory unchanged (spine misconception 2, §A7.2.3). A same-ID exclusive read moves the watch (§A7.2.1). An abandoned pair keeps being watched (§A7.2.2). A neighbouring write inside a monitored block larger than the access fails a 'successful' exclusive (§A7.2.4, up to 128 bytes).

A 128-byte memory strip draws each ID's watched span as a bracket, so the learner can see the watch being moved or ended. The lesson would embed it as <ExclusiveAccessVisualizer initialPreset="unpaired-write" /> under the corner cases.

needs.where: Exclusive restrictions list (lines 254-259) and the 'Debug: bad exclusive' situation
needs.concept: The A7.2.4 shape rules: total bytes a power of two, at most 128, at most 16 beats in AXI4, address aligned to the total, the write identical to the read (address, ID, size, length, control), and a non-cacheable AxCACHE so the monitor sees the access. Breaking any of them is UNPREDICTABLE, and a checker must flag the cause.

needs.where: ### Who checks what: the responsibility matrix (L101-127), between the three design decisions and the table; the Recap table (L655-664) reuses the result
needs.concept: A check belongs where its information is. Pins at a few edges go to a checker assertion; the request's ID, length or address to the monitor; expected data to the scoreboard; addresses, data and B times to the reference model; a product contract to the performance monitor. A check in the wrong place cannot see what it needs, or fires on legal traffic.

Feedback states what goes wrong in the wrong place, for example 'an assertion sees only RID, not which same-ID read the data belongs to' or 'a data-checking monitor cannot be reused across an interconnect', and cites the clause. needs.where: ### Error responses: legal, recorded, judged elsewhere (L409-459), after the 'Who decides what about that SLVERR' table (L449-455)
needs.concept: SLVERR and DECERR are legal responses (§A3.4.4, encodings in Table A3-4). The monitor records them, the reference model predicts them, and the scoreboard judges each beat: the response first, RDATA only on OKAY/EXOKAY beats. An error never shortens a burst. Protocol misuse is flagged by a check, not by recording responses. EXOKAY means a successful exclusive access (§A3.4.4, §A7.2).
needs.interaction: A four-beat read strip. The learner sets the predicted response per beat (programmed error window, or DECERR for an unmapped address) and the slave's actual behaviour per beat: RRESP; RDATA as reference, zeros or stale; a burst ended early after the error; EXOKAY on a normal read. Before the reveal they predict, for each component, whether it reports and with which tag: monitor RLAST or nothing; scoreboard 'beat k resp', 'beat k data' or 'beat count'; test policy for an unpredicted error. The reveal runs a port of the Make It Work diff() and on_r_beat and prints the exact message strings. A 'monitor flags SLVERR' toggle shows that misconception failing every error-injection run. Accuracy note: the Make It Work checker has no EXOKAY or early-termination assertion. In that bench an early RLAST is caught by the monitor's RLAST check, and the model must say so rather than invent a checker hit.

textHeavy: Lines 26-36, ## Quick Take + 'You will be able to' (~465 words): what a bridge is (slave on one bus, master on the other), the AHB pipeline vs five AXI channels, why bridge bugs cost a lot, the freight-broker analogy and where it breaks, four objectives. There is no picture of the two buses or of the bridge's four jobs.

Lines 40-54, ### Words you need first + the start of ### Where bridges sit (~345 words): a glossary (master/slave, transfer/beat/burst, AHB address and data phase with HREADYOUT, the 1KB and 4KB boundary rules, posted vs non-posted, reference model, CDC). Every term could be a picture but is given only as text.

Lines 198-211, the undefined-INCR 'Check your prediction' + **Width conversion and WRAP** + 'Use the explorer now' (~395 words): when AWLEN can be known, downsizing (A4.3.1 Note), and a doubleword WRAP16 on a 32-bit AXI bus becoming one INCR (start at 0x0100) or two INCR16 (start at 0x0140).

Lines 230-242, ### AXI to AHB: what forces a split or a reshape (~380 words): the 1KB split of an INCR16 at 0x03F0, the most pieces per transfer size (2/3/4), FIXED, WRAP2, unaligned start, sparse/all-zero WSTRB, then 'Scroll back to the explorer above'.

Lines 420-424, end of ### Posted and non-posted writes (~280 words, about the threshold): early write response tied to HPROT[2] (Table 3-5) and AXI Device Non-bufferable (A4.4.1), the 16-wait-state cost (§5.1.2 Note), and the read-after-write ordering AHB requires vs what AXI gives (§3.8.4, §3.8.5, A5.3.4).

Lines 506-519, CDC pitfall + **Resets** + **Verifying CDC** + the CDC log signature + start of ### Verifying a bridge (~450 words): synchronizing VALID/READY/data bit by bit, AXI (A3.1.2) vs AHB (§7.1.2) reset rules, one side resetting with transfers in flight, CDC sign-off, and what a CDC bug looks like in a log.

Lines 635-639, ### Verifying a bridge after the scoreboard code (~290 words, about the threshold): response checks against the posting policy, read ordering check, checkers on each port tagged [Protocol]/[Policy], why no passive assertion sees WVALID waiting for AWREADY, control-field check intro.

Lines 969-1028, Make It Work 'Prove it can fail', 'How to use it in a bridge testbench', the checklist, then ## Push Further: Expert undefined-length INCR, early termination, what a bridge may change by memory type, posted writes ordering and latency, and the strobes intro (~1,500 words, the longest stretch in the lesson): four INCR policies, AXI padding with all strobes low and dropping R beats, Modifiable/Device modification rules (A4.3.1 Table A4-2, §3.8.4, §3.8.5), read/write order before BRESP (A5.3.4, A6.1), the posting promise (A6.4, A6.5).

Lines 1038-1071, strobes atomicity note + ### Expert: exclusive and locked accesses + ### Expert: AXI ID assignment + ### Expert: reset domain crossing + start of ### Expert: formal (~880 words): exclusives over AHB-Lite and AHB5, HMASTLOCK with no AXI4 equivalent, ID policies and split-read reordering (A5.3.1, A5.3.5), RDC release order, assume-guarantee and fairness.
Lines 1085-1102, end of Expert: formal (over-constraint, tracked byte, convergence) + ### Expert: performance and sizing + interview intro (~410 words).

Lines 1362-1398, Kata split-table note + ### Kata: plan the verification of a bridge, with most of its worked answer inside a details reveal (~625 words): posting per region (UART Device Non-bufferable vs SRAM Bufferable), error injection, CDC and reset scenarios, scoreboard scope.

Lines 1432-1447, debug challenge worked solution + lab paragraph (~300 words, borderline): stale-read cause, A5.3/A5.3.4/A6.1, two fixes. (Lines 1451-1472, References, ~630 words, are citations rather than teaching prose and need no visual.)

needs.where: ### AXI to AHB, 'Sparse or all-zero WSTRB' (line 240) and ### Expert: strobes, alignment and narrow transfers (lines 1026-1038)
needs.concept: An IHI0033B.b slave has no strobes: each enabled-byte run becomes the largest aligned AHB transfers that cover it, an all-zero transfer is skipped, and more than one piece loses single-copy atomicity (A7.1). In the other direction, a narrow AHB transfer sets the WSTRB lanes of its own address (A3.4.3).

needs.where: **The length nobody told the bridge** (lines 176-203) + ### Expert: undefined-length INCR (992-1000) + ### Expert: early termination on AHB, none on AXI (1002-1008)
needs.concept: With an undefined-length INCR the bridge cannot know AWLEN/ARLEN until the burst ends (Table 3-3, §3.5.1). Each of the four policies has a cost. Once announced, an AXI burst cannot be cut short (A3.4.1): unwanted W transfers go out with all strobes low and unwanted R beats are dropped. Speculative reads are allowed only for Modifiable or Normal memory (A4.3.1, §3.8.5) and never for Device memory (§3.8.4).
needs.interaction: Scrub an AHB INCR edge by edge (NONSEQ, SEQ, BUSY, then SEQ or IDLE as the learner chooses). At each edge the learner commits 'can AWLEN be fixed now?' before the reveal. They then pick a policy (single-transfer, buffer to end/1KB/256, fixed INCR4 chunks, speculative read), a memory type (Device vs Normal/Modifiable) and 'master cancels after beat k'. They see the AXI AW/W or AR/R stream the policy produces: padding transfers with WSTRB=0, WLAST on transfer AWLEN+1, dropped R beats, a latency count, and a [Protocol] flag on a speculative Device read.

needs.where: ### Responses and errors, both directions (lines 261-358)
needs.concept: How responses map in each direction: RRESP per beat vs one BRESP per write burst after the last W (A3.4.4, A3.3.1). The two-cycle AHB ERROR (§5.1.3). The master cancels or continues (§3.5.2). Every R beat is still accepted. An AXI-to-AHB bridge folds every AHB ERROR into one BRESP. SLVERR vs DECERR is a documented policy.
needs.interaction: Pick a direction, read or write, the error beat k, SLVERR or DECERR, and whether the AHB master cancels or continues. Predict three things before the reveal: the edge at which the master first learns of the error, what RRESP or BRESP the AXI master sees, and which R beats the bridge drops. Then step through a two-bus CycleWaveform where AHB and AXI rows read the same model step. The lesson's two static waveforms become presets.

needs.where: ### AXI handshake dependencies: the bridge's own deadlock (lines 451-473, after the SequenceDiagram)
needs.concept: As an AXI master the bridge must not make WVALID wait for AWREADY, while a legal slave may wait for WVALID before AWREADY (A3.3.1 and its Caution). A bench that ties AWREADY high hides the bug.
needs.interaction: Choose which signals wait for which on the master side and the slave side, predict 'deadlocks / latent violation / safe', then see the wait-for graph and its loop. Then switch the slave to 'AWREADY waits for AWVALID' and watch the same buggy bridge pass: the latent violation a tied-high bench hides.

needs.where: ### What differs between AHB and AXI: control-field table (lines 104-119) + bug-table row 'Control fields mapped wrongly' (line 798)
needs.concept: Mapping HPROT to AxPROT/AxCACHE: AxPROT[2] = !HPROT[0], AxPROT[0] = HPROT[1], AxCACHE[0] = HPROT[2], AxCACHE[1] = HPROT[3]. The AHB memory type comes from Table 3-6. AxPROT[1] and AxCACHE[3:2] are a system choice unless the bridge has the AHB5 HNONSEC / Extended_Memory_Types properties.
needs.interaction: Toggle HPROT[3:0] (HPROT[6:4] = 0). See AxPROT/AxCACHE, the AHB memory type name (Device-nE, Device-E, Normal Non-cacheable) and whether an early write response is permitted. Then turn on a bug (AxPROT[2] copied instead of inverted, or AxCACHE[0] tied high) and predict the downstream symptom (an access filter answering DECERR, or a 'write then poll status' sequence reading stale status) before the reveal.

needs.where: ### Clocks and resets: asynchronous bridges and the bit-by-bit pitfall (lines 479-515)
needs.concept: Why only Gray-coded FIFO pointers cross, through two-flop synchronizers, while the payload stays in the FIFO memory. Why synchronizing VALID, READY and the data bits separately gives VALID with half-updated data, missed pulses and double counts.
needs.interaction: Two clock lanes with ratio and phase controls. Pointer mode: the write pointer steps from 3 to 4 (binary 011->100, Gray 010->110). The learner predicts which values the reading domain may capture if it samples inside the transition window. Reveal: with binary, any of the 8 bit mixes is possible (false full or empty); with Gray, only the old or the new value. Separate-sync mode: VALID and each data bit get their own skew, and the learner sees VALID arrive with stale data bits and a one-cycle pulse from the faster clock vanish.

Predict which of the five checks fire, then reveal the model's verdict per check. The 0x03F0 room+1 mutant visibly crosses the 1KB fence with a 5-transfer first burst.

needs.concept: |-> starts the consequent at the antecedent's end point (§16.12.7) and s_eventually counts the current tick (§16.12.13), so 'NONSEQ |-> s_eventually HREADY' passes on a hung data phase. needs.where: ### Verifying a bridge: formal setup (lines 693-740) + ### Expert: formal verification of a bridge that converges (1066-1090)
needs.concept: Assume the environment and assert the bridge (§16.14.1, §16.14.2). Without fairness, a silent slave is a counterexample to every liveness property. needs.where: ### Expert: what a bridge may change, by memory type (lines 1010-1016)
needs.concept: Which transformations a bridge may make for each memory type. Under AXI A4.3.1 Table A4-2, a Non-modifiable transaction keeps its parameters (except an INCR longer than 16 may be split and downsizing forces a modification). Under AHB5, Device memory may be broken into smaller bursts with the same transfer count and the same HSIZE, with no write merging (§3.8.4); Normal memory may change HBURST and HSIZE (§3.8.5).
needs.interaction: Predict-grid exercise. Rows: split INCR > 16, split at 1KB keeping size, merge SINGLEs, change HSIZE, prefetch read, early write response. Columns: Device-nE, Device-E, Normal Non-modifiable/Modifiable. The learner marks each cell allowed or forbidden, then reveals each cell with the clause that governs it and which spec it comes from. The lesson's 'author's reading' cell stays labelled as such.

staticVisuals: ## Quick Take (after line 30): a one-glance kit ArchitectureDiagram 'One bridge, two buses': the AHB side (address/control bus, HWDATA, HRDATA, pipelined) feeds a bridge drawn as slave | master, which drives the five AXI channels AW/W/B/AR/R. The bridge's four jobs are labelled on it: reshape bursts, map responses, choose posting, cross clocks.

### Words you need first (lines 46-47): a TimingDiagram of two AHB transfers with overlapping address and data phases and one HREADYOUT wait state (next address held). Beside it, a static address line with dashed 1KB fences and a solid 4KB fence captioned 'every 4KB boundary is a 1KB boundary'. This is the shared anchor the whole lesson refers back to.
### AHB to AXI, 'Never 4KB' (line 163): a predict-then-check prompt before the rule: 'Can a legal AHB INCR ever cross a 4KB boundary?'

**Width conversion and WRAP** (lines 207-209): a beat-order table comparing the doubleword WRAP16 at 0x0140 (order 0x140...0x178, then 0x100...0x138) with the two INCR16 bursts of words (bytes 0x0140-0x017F, then 0x0100-0x013F). Add a row for the start at 0x0100 (one INCR of 32 words).

After ### The two mistakes everyone makes (line 256): a split-decision step reveal for both directions. AHB->AXI: input legal under 1KB? -> width conversion? -> WRAP longer than 16 after downsizing? -> more than 256 transfers? AXI->AHB: FIXED? WRAP2? unaligned? sparse WSTRB? crosses 1KB? Each step cites its clause.

### AXI to AHB (line 232): a TimingDiagram of the AHB master port for the 0x03F0 split: INCR4 at 0x03F0-0x03FC, then a NONSEQ at 0x0400 starting a new INCR, with a marker 'new burst at the 1KB boundary'.

### AXI to AHB, 'How many pieces at most?' (line 234): a predict-first prompt, then a table of transfer size (4 bytes or less / 8 / 16) -> maximum span of an aligned 256-transfer INCR (1KB / 2KB / 4KB) -> most AHB pieces (2 / 3 / 4).

### Responses and errors (after line 335, before the SequenceDiagram): a predict prompt ('when and how does the AXI master hear about an AHB ERROR on transfer 2?'), plus a TimingDiagram for the AXI-to-AHB read direction: the two-cycle AHB ERROR on transfer 2 maps to RRESP=SLVERR on R beat 2, and every remaining R beat is still returned under the documented policy.
### Posted and non-posted writes (line 420): a table mapping memory type (AHB Table 3-6 / AXI Table A4-5) -> early write response permitted? -> posting allowed? -> clause (Table 3-5, A4.4.1).
### AXI handshake dependencies (lines 453-455): a two-column table, 'bridge as AXI master' vs 'bridge as AXI slave', listing what each may wait for and must not wait for (A3.3.1).

### Clocks and resets, the bit-by-bit pitfall (line 506): a TimingDiagram, badged as an illustration, of separately synchronized VALID and data bits. VALID reaches the ACLK domain one cycle before data bit 3 does. The caption says it shows bit skew, not metastability. Add a predict prompt before it.

### Clocks and resets, **Resets** (lines 508-511): an AXI (A3.1.2) vs AHB (§7.1.2) reset comparison table covering assertion, deassertion, what masters drive, what slaves drive, and the earliest transfer after reset. needs.concept: How one line moves through two caches, the interconnect and memory: which request transaction a load or store needs, which snoop the interconnect sends, which CRRESP answers the snooped cache may legally give, the RRESP[3:2] the requester gets, and where the duty to update memory sits (it never disappears: a cache or the interconnect always holds it).
needs.interaction: New AceCoherencyTraceLab (model src/lib/ace-coherency-model.ts, a deterministic educational model). The learner picks the next event: A or B load, partial store, full-line store or evict, or a DMA ReadOnce or MakeInvalid. The learner predicts in stages: the request (ReadShared, ReadUnique, CleanUnique, MakeUnique, WriteBack, Evict, or none for a store to UC/UD, C4.3.2); the snoop (Table C5-1); then the snooped cache's answer, picked from the legal rows only (Tables C5-7 ReadOnce, C5-8 ReadClean/ReadNotSharedDirty/ReadShared, C5-9 ReadUnique, C5-10 CleanInvalid, C5-11 MakeInvalid, C5-12 CleanShared, all checked in IHI0022E). The interconnect also has the legal choice to write the dirty line back itself and give PassDirty=0 (C6.4, Table C6-2). Reveal: each cache gets a state chip with non-colour cues for Unique/Shared and Clean/Dirty; the panel shows the CRRESP and RRESP bits, the memory value and the golden value, a single 'owes memory' token that moves between A, B, the interconnect and nobody, and the global checker's verdict naming the C1.2.3 rule. A scrubber steps through the trace, with a What/Why sentence and the clause for each step. An ownership-timeline log uses the lesson's `COH line=...` format. A snoop-filter toggle switches between the legal end-state sets of Tables C4-9 and C4-10. Presets for each lesson use: readshared-dirty (all three legal answers of Table C5-8 for UD), store-cleanunique, run1, run2, readonce-mutant (illegal mapping, Table C5-2), makeinvalid-vanishing, readclean-passdirty (the interconnect owes memory, C1.4.2/C3.7), snoop-crosses-writeback (C5.2.3).

needs.concept: The crossbar W-ordering deadlock has three ingredients. Each master sends W in its own AW order (§A5.4.1). Each slave takes W in its AW grant order (§A5.3.2). With no W buffering, opposite grant orders close a cycle of waits that one-master block tests cannot form.
needs.interaction: The learner sets each master's AW issue order, each slave's grant order, W buffering (none, or one burst per master port) and an optional mitigation: order AW acceptances, or a slave that takes an AW only with its W. They predict 'deadlocks' or 'completes'. The reveal draws the wait-for graph with the loop highlighted and steps the W beats one at a time. The default preset is the interview scenario: A to S1 then S0, B to S0 then S1, S0 grants A first, S1 grants B first, no buffering. Changing one grant order, or adding the one-burst buffer, completes the run. Label the mitigations as implementation choices, as B-AXI-5 does. B-AXI-5 can reuse it.

needs.concept: Spine misconception 3: the same seed reproduces a failure after a rebuild. Under SystemVerilog object stability (§18.14), a new object's RNG is seeded with the next random value from the thread that creates it, so an object created earlier in the run shifts the seeds of every later object in that thread. Objects created after existing ones keep stability. In UVM, components, sequences started on a sequencer and sequence items are also reseeded by type name and full name when UVM seeding is on (uvm-core uvm_object::reseed / uvm_create_random_seed), which protects them but not plain objects, threads or $urandom.

Each thread has its own RNG, and $urandom, std::randomize(), new and fork take that thread's next value in order (IEEE 1800-2023 §18.14.1 hierarchical seeding and object stability, §18.14.2). UVM seeds objects by type and full name, not allocation order (IEEE 1800.2-2020 Annex F.4.1.4.26 / §5.3.3.3), and uvm-core reseeds each item in start_item. Report messages preserve the caller's state (§6.2.2.2); user-code hooks such as sprint() are not guaranteed to (§1.4.6).

A stored handle also makes item reuse corrupt every queued item.

needs.concept: One owner per item. kill() leaves the held item in the request FIFO: uvm-core's kill_sequence() calls remove_sequence_from_queues() and m_kill(). stop_sequences() flushes m_req_fifo, so a later item_done() is UVM_FATAL SQRBADITMDN, and the stopped flag is the fix. A callback returns to the driver and cannot end a sequence. A sequence that ignores BUS_DROPPED loops in zero time, so simulated time stops. This is the assessment misconception 'callbacks can abort a running sequence'.

Predict the outcome: clean end, SQRBADITMDN fatal, sequence stuck in finish_item(), or zero-time loop. Then step the sequencer's request FIFO, arbitration queue and sequence state, with the uvm-core log line at each step.

No visual before BeforeYouStart.

needs.concept: Synchronization points: every edge, delay or signal change that host code waits on is a host-emulator round trip. Moving the timed code into an HDL-side BFM collapses one burst to one call. A monitor on pins forces a sync on every clock; a proxy that pulls costs a call per burst; a BFM that pushes through a back-pointer costs one void call.
needs.interaction: New component (for example CoEmulationSyncVisualizer + src/lib/co-emulation-model.ts, reusing simulateChannels from src/lib/axi-channel-model.ts for the AW/W/B handshake edges). Controls: slave behaviour (beats 1-8, AWREADY delay, WREADY stalls per beat, B latency; preset = the lesson DUT); driver style (host pin-level drive_burst | HDL BFM task write_burst | SCE-MI function-only start_burst + burst_done callback); monitor style (host pin-level | proxy pulls a BFM task | BFM pushes a void function); clock generator in hvl_top or hdl_top. The learner predicts the number of host-emulator synchronizations for one burst before the reveal. Then a PlaybackControls scrubber steps a two-lane host/emulator swimlane: each crossing is numbered, the emulator lane is shaded 'time frozen' while host code runs, a CycleWaveform shows the handshakes, and the code panel highlights the line that is waiting. A tally splits the count by source (align, AW, W beats, stalls, B, monitor, clock). Presets: lesson burst (8 waits vs 1 call), long burst with stalls, monitor on pins, monitor pull, monitor push, HVL clock generator, SCE-MI function-only. Accuracy: (1) count distinct synchronization moments. An edge on which the driver and the monitor both wait is one moment, so a pin-level monitor adds syncs only on edges the driver does not wait on (idle gaps between bursts); the Debrief's 'adds one per clock on top' needs this precision. (2) Handshake rule from IHI0022E §A3.2.1; sampling and drive timing from IEEE 1800-2023 §14.3 and §14.16 (both checked). (3) Frozen time (SCE-MI 2.4 §4.4.4) and functions-only (§5.6.3.1.4) are not in the local source set, so encode only what the lesson states. (4) Veloce TBX non-blocking one-way calls: leave this out, or make it an off-by-default toggle labelled tool-dependent. Fidelity: deterministic educational model for the counts. Keyboard: arrow keys step; reduced motion is stepped only.

needs.where: Push Further > Expert: Throughput engineering (1048-1056, inside the 1,100-word stretch 1039-1088); also serves the debug table rows at 494-497 and the interview 'the bench that only got 3x faster' (1089-1098)
needs.concept: Run time is about (emulated cycles / emulator clock) + (synchronizations x (link latency + host work per sync)). Whichever term dominates decides the fix: a sync-bound run needs fewer syncs, a host-bound run needs less host work per sync (time is frozen meanwhile), and an emulation-bound run needs a faster platform or fewer cycles.

Then a stacked time bar shows the three terms with a verdict chip (sync-bound / host-bound / emulation-bound) and the lesson's matching fix. needs.where: Build Your Mental Model > Packing order across the boundary (372-380, comparison table)
needs.concept: A packed struct is one vector whose first member is the most significant (IEEE 1800-2023 §7.2.1). It reaches C as canonical svBitVecVal words, the first element holding the 32 LSBs, with undetermined unused bits in the last element (Annex H.7.7, checked). A naive C struct therefore reads idNum from the low byte of value, and value from the word that holds idNum.
needs.interaction: A bit strip of the 40-bit {idNum, value} vector with coloured fields, cut into word 0 and word 1 (the 24 unused upper bits of word 1 hatched as 'undetermined', not zero). Below it, the C struct's byte map (stated assumption: little-endian, natural alignment, padding hatched). The learner edits idNum and value, toggles the C field order (naive / reversed / pack with svGetPartselBit), and predicts what C reads for each field; the reveal draws arrows from bytes to fields. Accuracy: the lesson's 'value reads the word that holds idNum (1 in its low byte)' is right only for the low byte, because H.7.7 makes the upper bits undetermined, so the visual must not show them as 0. The C layout depends on the ABI and must be labelled as an assumption. SCE-MI 2.4 §5.6.1.3.3 is not in the local sources.
needs.gap: Closest is DPIBoundaryInspector, which maps a packed struct to svBitVecVal but shows no bit or byte layout. This could be added there as a 'packed struct layout' scenario instead of as a new component.

needs.where: Push Further > Expert: SCE-MI pipes and batching (1044-1046); also the Pipes paragraph (405) and the 'Three ways across' SequenceDiagram (407-424)
needs.concept: Transaction pipes are one-way. In deferred visibility the infrastructure may buffer elements, and the consumer sees them only once the pipe fills or is flushed; in immediate visibility the consumer sees each element the next time it gets control. flush guarantees the reader has consumed the data. Batching lets many items share one synchronization, at the cost of latency and a harder end of test.
needs.interaction: The learner issues N non-blocking sends and picks the visibility mode and pipe depth, then predicts 'how many items has the HDL consumer seen?' and 'is it safe to run check_phase now?'. Stepping through shows the buffer filling, the synchronizations counted, flush returning once the items are consumed, and a 'scoreboard: pending items' warning if the test ends before the flush. A side toggle contrasts this with one function call per item. Fidelity: conceptual illustration, because deferred buffering is permitted ('may'), not mandated. Claims are limited to SCE-MI 2.4 §4.8.1 and §4.8.8 as the lesson quotes them; the standard is not in the local source set.

needs.concept: 4-state vs 2-state engines. An X from an un-reset flop propagates in simulation and trips a check; on a 2-state engine it becomes 0 or 1 and the check can pass. SCE-MI coerces X to 1 and Z to 0 for values arriving from the software side.

needs.where: What you read and write after each trigger (the timing model), L92-115; and Push Further 'Expert: where cocotb triggers land in the SystemVerilog scheduler', L942-954
needs.concept: What a trigger means in cocotb: awaiting a trigger registers one VPI callback reason, the reason sits at a point on the IEEE 1800-2023 time-slot ladder, and that point decides what a read returns and when a default write reaches the DUT. Two examples: RisingEdge gives the old flop output and its write lands at the next edge; ReadOnly sits in Postponed, where a write is an error.
needs.interaction: A time-slot ladder that reuses visuals/scheduler/RegionLadder and REGION_ORDER, with the PLI points of §4.4.3 inserted (Pre-Active, Pre-NBA, Post-NBA, Postponed) and cocotb's five phase names on a side rail. The learner picks a trigger (Timer, NextTimeStep, RisingEdge, ReadWrite, ReadOnly), an action (read flop output q, or write push = 1) and a simulator kind (event-driven or Verilator). They first predict whether the read returns the old or the new q, and whether the DUT sees push at this edge, at the next edge, or never because a RuntimeError is raised. Then they step with PlaybackControls: clk value change (cbValueChange has no Table 4-1 row and fires on the change), coroutine resumed (▶ at Values Change), write queued (◆ pending), always_ff runs and NBA updates q, cbReadWriteSynch applies the queued write, then Postponed (write marked illegal per §4.4.2.9). The ReadWrite preset shows a 'Scheduler choice: Pre-NBA or Post-NBA' badge with both outcomes and never picks one. The Verilator preset adds the implicit ReadWrite after the edge trigger, so q reads as the new value. The COCOTB_TRUST_INERTIAL_WRITES preset ends in 'simulator-dependent', not in an edge number. Presets: read-after-RisingEdge, write-after-RisingEdge, write-in-ReadOnly, ReadWrite ambiguity, Verilator, trusted inertial writes.

No model knows cocotb triggers, write queueing or Verilator's edge handling. It needs a new src/lib/cocotb-timing-model.ts built on sv-scheduler-model's REGION_ORDER. Accuracy: I verified the LRM side locally (§4.10 Table 4-1: cbAfterDelay and cbNextSimTime in Pre-Active, cbReadWriteSynch in Pre-NBA or Post-NBA, cbReadOnlySynch in Postponed; §4.4.3; §4.4.2.9). needs.concept: Every rising edge with VALID and READY both HIGH is a separate transfer, so holding AWVALID (with AWADDR) and WVALID until BVALID gives a duplicate write whenever the slave raises AWREADY again. Whether the bug shows depends on a slave choice the protocol does not require. This is spine misconception 3.

A slave toggle (slave A: AWREADY at edges 2 and 4; slave B: AWREADY low until after the B transfer) shows why the same test passes on one slave and fails on the other. A 'Fix' toggle replays with each VALID dropped after its own handshake (the lesson's 'Right' figure).

needs.where: Where your Python runs: inside the simulator, L58-90; What Python costs, and why, L370-376; Push Further 'Expert: performance', L968-979
needs.concept: One operating-system process. Simulated time stops while Python runs (a breakpoint or a NumPy loop freezes the simulation), and the bench's cost grows with trigger wake-ups and GPI signal accesses per cycle, not with the DUT. Spine misconception 1: cocotb does not run the DUT in Python.
needs.interaction: Two lanes: simulator kernel in simulated ns, Python in wall-clock steps. The learner picks a bench (thin bench: one wake-up per transaction; polling bench: five coroutines waking on every edge and reading 20 signals each; breakpoint held) and toggles levers: wait for the event instead of polling, read the bus once, Clock(impl="gpi"), trusted inertial writes, transaction-level BFM in HDL. They first predict whether simulated time advances during the Python segment, and which lever removes the most crossings for this bench. Then they see the simulated-time lane stay flat during every Python segment, and a counter of callbacks plus GPI accesses per simulated cycle (and per transaction) fall with each lever. It shows counts only and never claims a slowdown factor or seconds, because the lesson states that no fixed factor exists. Fidelity: illustration of the counting model.

needs.where: Coroutines and tasks versus fork and join, L146-178 (mapping table and the start_soon/await SequenceDiagram)
needs.concept: Cooperative concurrency. start_soon is fork…join_none and runs at the next scheduling point. gather is join. select is join_any but cancels the losers, which SV join_any does not do. task.cancel() kills one process. When the test coroutine returns, cocotb cancels every running Task, including a monitor that is mid-transfer.
needs.interaction: SV and cocotb lanes side by side for the same two processes (one finishes at 30 ns, the other at 50 ns), plus a monitor Task. The learner picks a construct pair (join_none/start_soon, join/gather, join_any/select, end of test with the monitor running) and first predicts: after the fast process finishes, is the slow one still running? Does the monitor see the last transfer? Then the lanes show SV's join_any leaving the slow process running (IEEE 1800-2023 §9.3.2 Table 9-1), cocotb's select ending it with a CancelledError marker, and the test's return cutting the monitor lane mid-transfer.
needs.existing: ForkJoinVisualizer scenario="join-variants" (SV lanes from sv-process-model)
needs.gap: SV code and semantics only. It needs a cocotb code variant and a small cocotb task model for start_soon timing, select cancellation and cancel-at-test-end (cocotb 2.0 PR 4574; 2.1 PRs 5165 and 5206; check against the cocotb 2.1 docs, which are outside the provided source set). Accuracy: the lesson's row 'disable fork (one process) → task.cancel()' needs care. §9.6.3 says disable fork terminates all descendant subprocesses of the calling process. The one-process SV counterpart is the process class's kill() (§9.7), which also kills that process's own descendants. The visual should show this correctly.

needs.where: ### Expert: Data conversion, byte order and packing (lines 672-690), before the traced-example table. Absorbs the text-heavy stretch at lines 668-681.
needs.concept: Why fields come out reversed or scrambled across a boundary. The first member of a packed struct is the most significant (IEEE 1800-2023 §7.2.1). DPI passes packed vectors as canonical svBitVecVal chunks, with element 0 holding the 32 LSBs (Annex H.7.7). A C struct puts its first member at the lowest address. Generic payload data byte order is left to the user (1800.2 §12.3.4.2.9). do_pack has a fixed field order and does not pack extensions (§12.3.4.2.4).
needs.interaction: Tab 1: the learner edits a packed struct (default cmd_t with opcode 8'h5A and addr 24'h001234; fields, widths and values are editable) and predicts what opcode reads after memcpy into a C struct. They then see the SV bit strip, MSB first and coloured by field; the c[0] chunk; the host bytes at offsets 0-3; the C fields after memcpy (opcode 0x34); and the C fields after shift-and-mask (0x5A, 0x001234). Tab 2: the learner picks a byte order for each side of a generic payload data array, writes 0xCAFEF00D, and predicts the word the other side reads. Tab 3: the do_pack field order as a strip, with an extension that silently does not travel.

needs.concept: Lock-step co-simulation. The ISS steps once per RTL retirement. Asynchronous events must be forwarded before the step, because the ISS takes a pending interrupt at the start of the step. Counters are overridden and bus errors are notified. A hung core produces no step and therefore no mismatch (misconception 3 and the hang pitfall).

Before stepping, the learner predicts the run result: all match, first mismatch at pc X, silent green, or TEST TIMEOUT fatal. Each step carries What/Why narration naming the governing DPI call. needs.where: ### RVFI and riscv-formal: the RVFI table and the TimingDiagram (lines 409-441)
needs.concept: RVFI packet rules. The other signals are meaningful only when rvfi_valid is 1. rvfi_order is unique with no gaps, however many cycles each retirement takes. rvfi_intr marks the first handler instruction (pc_rdata differs from the previous pc_wdata). rvfi_rd_wdata is 0 when rd is x0. After an interrupt, mepc holds the displaced instruction's address.
needs.interaction: An editable version of the lesson's RVFI waveform. Built on CycleWaveform with editable cells.
